First the wrong is named to the people who did it, and named as a wrong against themselves before it is called a wrong against God. Then a specific remedy is demanded, not a general sorrow. Then, once the remedy is described, the verse reports the acceptance of the repentance and names the mercy behind it. The Book does not leave a person to guess whether the remedy worked; it tells him, so that the passage about the calf ends where this verse ends. Ibn ʿAbbās transmitted that those who had not worshipped the calf were set against those who had, so the public rupture made by the idol was answered within the same community.

**A WRONG NAMED AS AN INJURY TO THE SELF**

The first clause in the speech of Moses identifies the injury in a way that a modern reader may not expect. The people are told that they have wronged themselves, which places the damage inside the community rather than in a distant ledger. Idolatry in the Book is never only a mistake about metaphysics; it is the handing over of a person's own dignity to something that cannot carry it, and the consequences fall on the worshipper first. The language is the same the sūrah used when it described the man who traded guidance for error and lost his capital in the transaction. Moses also calls the people his people in the middle of the accusation, and the Book keeps the possessive as a small but deliberate comfort. The rebuke comes from someone who is still standing with them, and the remedy he prescribes is presented as being for their benefit rather than as a punishment owed to an offended authority. The verse's final clause confirms the tone, since the one who accepted the repentance is named as Most Merciful. The severity of the route and the mercy at the end of it are reported by the same sentence.

**ACCEPTING THE REMEDY THAT FITS**

The practical lesson for a reader whose failures are of a different kind is about accepting the remedy that fits his case rather than a remedy that preserves his comfort. The children of Israel were told to do something that cost them their attachment to the thing they had made, and the Book calls that cost the best option available. A person today is usually asked for something smaller: the thing returned, the relationship repaired, the practice resumed, the admission made out loud. The Book's account of the calf establishes a principle that the rest of the sūrah keeps applying. The repair is judged by whether it removes the wrong rather than by whether it is agreeable, which is why the verse can call a hard measure the best option available. One thing a reader can do in response is to take an old mistake and look at the remedy he has been avoiding rather than the one he has already performed. The comfortable half of a repair is usually the visible half, and the missing piece is what the story of the calf would call the calf itself. The Book is not asking for self-punishment, and it does not want a person to invent a severity for himself. It is asking for the specific removal of the specific thing, which is what the verse records and what the mercy at its end responds to. The reason acceptance is announced after the severe remedy is to prevent severity from becoming the final name of God in the account.

---

## Verse 2:55

> And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses! We will never believe you until we see Allah with our own eyes,” so a thunderbolt struck you while you were looking on

**A DEMAND TO SEE WHAT CANNOT BE SEEN**

The next scene opens with a demand that a reader has heard before in other mouths: ***“And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses!”***, ***“We will never believe you”***, ***“until we see Allah with our own eyes,””***, and then ***“so a thunderbolt struck you”***, ***“while you were looking on”***. The request is not for evidence; the sea had parted and the mountain had shaken in front of these people. What they demanded was a change in the terms of the relationship, since seeing God with their own eyes would have removed the element of trust that the whole arrangement rests on. The verse reports the answer without a word of commentary, and the answer is that the demand was met with a stroke that left them watching their own end. Ibn ʿAbbās understood the demand as a refusal to credit Moses until God was seen openly, and the thunderbolt as the fire that overtook the men while they watched.

The Book tells the same story in another sūrah with more of the exchange preserved, and the request there is repeated in a form that makes its nature plain: the people ask Moses to bring down a written revelation, and the Book records the escalation in their demands. The Qur'an treats this appetite as a recurring disease rather than a single event, and it names the condition in a passage about the same community: (4:153 — **“The People of the Book demand that you ˹O Prophet˺ bring down”**), with the rest of the verse listing the requests that followed. The reader is being shown what happens when a person decides that belief should be made easy on his own terms.

**A DEMAND THAT CONTRADICTS TRUST**

The request in this verse is often read as an excess of honesty, and the Book is clear that it is the opposite. A person who insists on seeing before he believes has already decided that the evidence available to him is not enough, and in this case the available evidence had been overwhelming. What the demand really asks for is a God who is available on command and a relationship without the risk of trust. That is a different religion from the one being offered, and it is the religion the sūrah has been describing since it named the people who say they believe while keeping their options open. The Book elsewhere states the principle that this scene illustrates, and it puts the sight of God at a distance no living person can cross: no eye can reach him in this world, and the request to try has been refused to everyone who asked. The verse does not explain this, and it does not need to. A reader who has understood that trust is the whole content of the relationship will see at once why the demand in the sentence had to be answered with a bolt rather than a demonstration.

**WANTING PROOF ON ONE'S OWN TERMS**

A reader can find this demand in his own week easily enough, because it takes the form of conditions. A person says that he would commit if he were shown a sign, that he would change if the evidence were stronger, that he would pray if he felt something. The Book has already given the evidence it intends to give, and the demand in this verse is the same demand in modern clothes. The lesson of the scene is not that questions are forbidden, since the sūrah itself has been answering them for fifty verses. The lesson is that a condition attached to obedience is a refusal in disguise. The practical step is to name one condition that is standing between a person and a decision, and to state honestly whether it is a genuine question or a way of postponing something already known. The people in this verse had an answer available to them all along, and the Book records that they were looking on when it arrived. A reader who notices the same posture in himself has learned the lesson of the passage without having to receive the answer in their form. Present-day demands for proof can carry the same defect when a person rejects every kind of evidence except the one he has chosen in advance. The demand is like refusing a physician's diagnosis unless the patient can see the disease with an unaided eye. What turns on the demand is the difference between seeking evidence and dictating the only evidence that will be allowed to count.

---

## Verse 2:56

> Then We brought you back to life after your death, so that perhaps you would be grateful

**LIFE GIVEN BACK AFTER THE STROKE**

The scene of the demand has a sequel that the sūrah reports in one sentence: ***“Then We brought you back to life after your death”***, and ***“so that perhaps you would be grateful”***. Nothing is said about the interval, and the mechanism is not explained. It states that a dead people were revived, and then it attaches the usual purpose to the gift. Everything in the sentence is a repetition of the pattern the chapter has been building: a benefit given without a claim to it, and a purpose attached to the giving. The reader has seen the same ending after the crossing of the sea and after the pardon of the calf, and he is meant to recognise the refrain. Ibn ʿAbbās treated the words as an actual return to life after the men had died, making gratitude the required answer to a restored existence rather than to a narrow escape.

The closeness of the two verses is the point a reader should not miss. In one sentence the people demand to see God and are struck down; in the next they are given their lives back. The mercy follows the presumption immediately and without a probationary period, and the Book presents the sequence as a fact about how its Lord deals with a stubborn people. The same arrangement is repeated later in the sūrah when a shadow and a supply of food are described as favours given to the same community: (2:57 — **“And ˹remember when˺ We shaded you with clouds and sent down to you manna and quails, ˹saying˺,”**), and the sentence continues with the invitation to eat from what has been provided.

**A GIFT THAT CAME AFTER DEATH**

The Book keeps using death and revival as the plainest illustration of what it can do, and the reader is being taught to draw the conclusion rather than simply to marvel. A power that can return a person to his body after a bolt has killed him can also raise the whole of humanity at the end of time, and the argument from the smaller case to the larger runs through the Qur'an from beginning to end. The people in this scene were given a demonstration rather than a proof, which is exactly what they had demanded one verse earlier, and the Book notes the irony without comment. The second clause then names what the demonstration was for. The purpose is not that they would be convinced of a doctrine but that they would become grateful, which returns the reader to the theme the sūrah has been pressing since it described the favours of the exodus. Gratitude in the Book is the response that keeps a person in contact with reality, and a person who has been given his life back twice has more reason for it than anyone. The verse leaves the response open, as it must, and it names the response it hopes for.

**THE DEBT A SECOND CHANCE CREATES**

Every reader can find a version of this verse in his own history, since most people have been brought back from something: an illness, an accident, a decision that could have ended differently. The Book treats such recoveries as gifts and not as luck, and it asks the same thing of them that it asked of the people in this scene. The obligation is not a debt to be settled but a direction to be taken, and the sūrah will shortly spell out the direction in detail when it turns to the commands that follow. A reader can take the verse in hand by naming the second chance he has been given and the thing he intends to do with it, in one sentence, without decoration. The Book does not require a person to be afraid of the past; it requires him to be honest about the present. A life returned is a life that belongs to someone else, and the verse says so in the plainest way its wording allows. Today, recovery after a near-fatal illness should be read as renewed time for gratitude rather than as ownership of extra years. It is like receiving a house key after being carried from a fire: the returned shelter turns every ordinary room into a reason for thanks. The sequence also establishes resurrection by a witnessed event inside history. The people who returned were not brought back because death had been misdiagnosed; the verse deliberately places death before revival. That ordering means gratitude rests on power over death itself, and the later promise of a general rising is no larger in kind than the sign already shown here.

---

## Verse 2:57

> And ˹remember when˺ We shaded you with clouds and sent down to you manna and quails, ˹saying˺, “Eat from the good things We have provided for you.” The evildoers ˹certainly˺ did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves

**SHADE, FOOD, AND A WARNING ABOUT WHO WAS HARMED**

The favours continue with two provisions and a correction: ***“And ˹remember when˺ We shaded you with clouds”***, ***“and sent down to you manna”***, ***“and quails, ˹saying˺, “Eat from the good things We have provided”***, ***“for you.” The evildoers ˹certainly˺ did not wrong Us”***, ***“but wronged themselves”***. The scene is a wilderness with no shelter and no harvest, and the Book names the two things that were supplied: a moving roof and a daily food supply that arrived without cultivation or trade. The command that comes with the provision is not an obligation but an invitation to eat, which is the shape the sūrah gives to most of its favours. Then the sentence turns and tells the reader who loses when a gift is refused. That final clause is one of the most important statements in the chapter, and it recurs elsewhere whenever the Book discusses disobedience. The Book reports the same principle about the same community in another place when their requests for variety in food are answered with a rebuke, and the wording there returns to the same idea of self-injury. A reader might reasonably ask why the correction is placed immediately after the gift rather than later in the passage. The answer is that the gift and the refusal are the two halves of the same story, and the Book will not describe one without naming the effect of the other. Ibn ʿAbbās placed the cloud, the manna and the quails in the wilderness, and read the food as lawful provision whose misuse injured the recipients rather than the Provider.

**A PROVISION NAMED DOWN TO THE LAST BIRD**

Manna and quails are named rather than summarised because the detail is what makes the passage an argument. Bread that appears without sowing and birds that arrive without hunting are provisions a person cannot attribute to his own skill, and their arrival every morning for years was a standing demonstration of where the supply line came from. The Book is building a case with the history of a people who saw it. The reader is asked to notice that even under those conditions a community can find grounds for complaint, which is a fact about human beings rather than about that generation. The Book reports the same provisions in another account of the same years: (20:81 — **“˹saying,˺ “Eat from the good things We have provided for you, but do not transgress in them,”**). The shade is the same kind of evidence. A cloud that moves with a migrating people and keeps the sun off them is not weather; it is an arrangement, and the Book names it as such. The sūrah is not asking the reader to be impressed by the miraculous. It is asking him to recognise the ordinary version of the same arrangement in his own life, where the shelter over his head and the food on his table also arrive without his having made the rain or the soil. The wilderness story is being told so that the ordinary case can be seen for what it is.

**THE ONLY PERSON A REFUSAL DAMAGES**

The sentence about self-injury is the practical heart of the verse, since God needs nothing from his creatures and their refusal takes nothing from Him. The answer given here is that the harm stays with the one who refuses, which is why the Book can describe a command as being for the benefit of the commanded. The provision was designated for the people, and the warning is that whoever turns away from it is the one who goes hungry. Nothing about that arrangement flatters the creature, and nothing about it makes the Creator smaller. The test for a reader is in how he talks about his obligations. A person who treats them as a bill owed to someone who benefits from the payment will resent them; a person who understands that the payment is for his own advantage will use them. What is wanted is that he notice one thing he has been avoiding as though the avoidance cost God something, and to see that the loss is entirely his own. That recognition is the beginning of the gratitude the previous verse was asking for. In the present day, abundance is still wasted when entitlement makes ordinary provision appear beneath notice.

---

## Verse 2:58

> And ˹remember˺ when We said, “Enter this city and eat freely from wherever you please; enter the gate with humility, saying, ‘Absolve us.’ We will forgive your sins and multiply the reward for the good-doers.”

**A CITY, A GATE, AND ONE SENTENCE TO SAY**

A city gate now becomes the place where victory is tested through manner and speech: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We said, “Enter this city”***, ***“and eat freely from wherever you please”***, ***“enter the gate with humility, saying, ‘Absolve us.' We will forgive your sins”***, ***“and multiply the reward”***, ***“for the good-doers.””***. The command has three parts and each of them is a test in miniature. A place was given to them, the food in it was declared free, and the manner of entry was specified. What the verse is describing is not a military conquest but an admission, and the terms of admission are humility, a spoken request for pardon, and the promise of a reward for those who do good. The same scene appears elsewhere in wording close enough to establish that both accounts describe one event: the same city, the same freedom to eat, and the same requirement to lower themselves as they pass through the gate. The comparison matters because the sūrah is teaching the reader to recognise a pattern in the way God deals with people. A gift is placed in front of them, a small act of humility is asked for, and the response to the two together determines what happens next. Everything in the passage is arranged so that the test is easy to pass and impossible to mistake. Ibn ʿAbbās identified the town as Jericho and understood the required saying as a plea for sins to be removed, which joins bodily humility to a spoken confession of need. The event is retold with its two promised outcomes side by side: (7:161 — **“and enter the gate with humility. We will forgive your sins, ˹and˺ We will multiply the reward for the good-doers.”**).

**THE MANNER MATTERED MORE THAN THE CITY**

The manner of entry is the part of the command that carries the lesson, since the city and the food were gifts and the bowing was the response. A people who had been rescued from slavery and fed in the desert were now being given a home, and the instruction was to walk in asking for pardon rather than as conquerors. The Book is drawing a line under the whole story: everything they had was received, and the manner of the receiving was expected to show it. The same principle appears in the sūrah's description of the believers, who give from what they have been given and are certain about the return. A reader should also notice the wording of the request. The sentence they were told to say is short, and it asks for pardon rather than for the city, the food, or the victory. The Book puts the request for forgiveness at the head of the entry because the thing being repaired is the relationship, and the rest follows from it. The reward mentioned in the closing words of the promise is then described as multiplication, which means the arrangement does not operate on a strict exchange rate. Both halves of the sentence come from the same generosity.

**ENTERING WITH THE RIGHT WORDS**

How a person receives what he has been given is the question this line puts to him. A promotion, a house, a recovery, a new year: each of them can be entered either as a right one has earned or as something received from the one who arranges matters, and the difference shows up immediately in how the person speaks. The Book places the two possible postures side by side in the story, since the next verse records a community that changed the words it had been given. The instruction in this verse was small, which is exactly what makes the following failure so instructive. A reader can take the verse as a template for the things he enters this week: a job, a room, a conversation, a meal. The formula is not complicated, and the verse gives it in plain language. One sentence acknowledging who gave the thing, and then the use of it as a gift rather than as a possession. A person who does that at one threshold has kept the command of this verse, and he has done it in a manner the Book promises to reward. Like a guest lowering his head at a doorway and admitting the damage he caused, posture and words together show that entry is not a claim of entitlement.

---

## Verse 2:59

> But the wrongdoers changed the words they were commanded to say. So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them for their rebelliousness

**ONE WORD CHANGED AND A PUNISHMENT SENT**

The command of the previous verse is answered with a substitution: ***“But the wrongdoers changed the words they were commanded to say.”***, ***“So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them”***, ***“for their rebelliousness”***. The Book does not say that the people refused to enter the city. It says that they changed the words, which is a smaller act with a larger meaning. The same event is set out in another sūrah with the instruction that preceded it: (7:161 — **“And ˹remember˺ when it was said to them, “Enter this city ˹of Jerusalem˺ and eat from wherever you please. Say,”**). The sentence they had been told to say was an admission of need, and the substitution turned it into something else, so the posture of the entering changed while the entering itself continued. The punishment named in the second clause follows from that change rather than from an outright revolt. The same account is given in another sūrah with the alteration itself described, and the reports of the early teachers explain what the substitution involved: a phrase turned into its opposite, or a word twisted while the letter of the instruction was preserved. The Book's interest is not in the syllables they used. It is in the fact that a people who had been given an easy command found a way to comply with it while emptying it, and the punishment is attached to that manoeuvre. The verse is a warning about the kind of obedience that keeps the form and discards the meaning. Ibn ʿAbbās transmitted that the commanded plea was exchanged for a mocking word and that the descending punishment was a plague, so both the alteration and its consequence were public.

**A MOCKING CHANGE WITH A PUBLIC COST**

A reader may wonder why a few words would bring down a punishment from the heavens, and the answer is in the sentence that had been given to them. The words were an act of submission, and the point of submission is the surrender of the right to rephrase. A person who accepts a command and then alters it to suit himself has kept the appearance of obedience while recapturing the authority that the command was meant to take from him. That is why the Book treats the editing of the formula as rebellion, and it is why the same charge appears later in the chapter against people who distort the scripture with their own hands. The Book also shows what the substitution accomplished in the community, because a changed formula becomes a changed practice and then a changed community. The generation that rewrote the sentence would raise children who never knew the original, and the loss would look like tradition by the time anyone noticed. The Qur'an's attention to wording is therefore not pedantry; it is an early warning about a decay that begins in language and ends in worship. The punishment from the heavens is reported as the end of a process that started with a phrase.

**KEEPING THE FORM AND LOSING THE MEANING**

The practical lesson for a reader is to check where he has been substituting his own wording for what he was given. The substitutions are usually reasonable-sounding: a prayer said with attention elsewhere, a fast kept while the temper is not, a charity given for the audience, a testimony adjusted to the listeners. The Book's example is a community that was promised a reward for good-doing and changed a request for pardon into something else, and the mechanism is available to anyone who wants to use it. The verse attaches a price to the mechanism, and it attaches it without ambiguity. A reader can begin by choosing one practice he performs on most days and examining the words he uses in it, without changing anything yet. What is wanted is that he notice the gap between the form and the meaning, since that gap is where the rebellion of this verse lives. A person who restores one formula to its intended sense has done what the people in this story were told to do at the gate, and he has done it before the punishment rather than after it. Today, sacred language can be preserved on a page while its demand is edited out of contracts, policies and public conduct. It is like altering one line in a safety instruction until the sign remains polished but directs people toward danger.

---

## Verse 2:60

> And ˹remember˺ when Moses prayed for water for his people, We said, “Strike the rock with your staff.” Then twelve springs gushed out, ˹and˺ each tribe knew its drinking place. ˹We then said,˺ “Eat and drink of Allah’s provisions, and do not go about spreading corruption in the land.”

**A PRAYER FOR WATER ANSWERED OUT OF STONE**

The thirst of the wilderness is answered without rain, without a well, and without a cloud. The verse opens with a request made on behalf of a crowd: ***“And ˹remember˺ when Moses prayed”***, ***“for water for his people, We said, “Strike the rock with your staff.””*** The man who prays is the prophet himself, and the request is for the people rather than for himself, which is the first thing the verse shows about him. The answer does not come as a supply lowered from the sky but as an instruction given to him: a command that puts the outcome in his hand and ties it to an act he can perform. The staff he is told to use is the same staff that will later be raised over the sea, and the instrument is named so that the reader sees that the power is not in the wood. What he does with it is obedience, and what comes out of the stone is not his doing.

**TWELVE STREAMS FOR TWELVE FAMILIES**

The result is described with a precision that answers a practical problem: ***“Then twelve springs gushed out, ˹and˺ each tribe knew its drinking place. ˹We then said,˺ “Eat”***. A single spring would have served the crowd and would have turned every morning into a scramble; twelve of them, one to a tribe, removed the crowding along with the thirst. The same event is told again among the favours recounted to this people elsewhere, where the division into tribes and the water are placed in one breath: (7:160 — **“We divided them into twelve tribes—each as a community. And We revealed to Moses,”**). The detail fits the way this chapter treats its history, since the favours it lists are always shaped to the community's own arrangement, and the arrangement here is the twelve houses descended from one man. A reader who keeps that in view sees why the number matters: the gift was measured out to the people as a body with parts, and no part was left out.

**A STONE GIVING WHAT A WELL COULD NOT**

The verse leaves the shape of the stone and the size of the staff unmentioned, and the reports that fill those gaps were never meant to carry the weight of the event itself. The stone is described in one account attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās as a square block with three openings on each side, so that each tribe drank from its own mouth, while other narrations trace the staff back through the prophets to Adam. A reading that treats the wording as naming a kind of stone rather than one particular rock has been preferred by some scholars, on the ground that a command which works on any stone of that kind displays more power than one bound to a single known object. The size of the staff and the way it is said to have shone are reported too, and a reader may take such details for what they are worth without resting the verse upon them. What the Book itself insists on is the contrast that comes later in this sūrah, when hearts are described as harder than rock even though some rocks split and pour out water: (2:74 — **“Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder,”**). A stone produced streams on demand, and the people who drank from them would later prove harder than the stone they had struck.

**EATING, DRINKING, AND THE CORRUPTION THAT FOLLOWS**

The command that closes the verse carries two halves, and the second is the reason the first is mentioned at all: ***“and drink of Allah’s provisions”***, ***“and do not go about spreading corruption in the land.””*** Full stomachs are not the end of the matter, because a people who eat well and forget the giver has corrupted the thing they were given. The same pairing appears in the address to this community in another sūrah, where the provision and the warning are set side by side: (20:81 — **“˹saying,˺ “Eat from the good things We have provided for you,”**). The phrase rendered as spreading corruption carries the sense of an act that spoils what lies around the person doing it, whether by disobedience or by injustice to others, and the two are usually found together in a community that has stopped being grateful. The verse therefore ends where a reader's own life begins: water in the desert is a gift, and the gift creates an obligation to keep the ground it fell on in good order.

**WATER, ORDER, AND RESTRAINT**

There is a plain comparison here for anyone who has ever been given what he asked for and then grown bored with it. A family that prays through a hard month and is brought through it will sometimes attribute the relief to its own cleverness within a year, and the change of heart is invisible while it happens. The people in this story were given water out of rock, with no work of their own in the matter, and the verse still had to end with a warning against spreading corruption. That is a measure of how quickly a gift can be separated from the memory of the giver, and the danger does not belong to one nation only. The instruction about the staff is also worth keeping, because it shows what the answer required of Moses: he was told to act, not to wait for the water to appear beside him, and the acting cost nothing but obedience. A reader who takes that seriously will not look for the provision to arrive without the strike, nor treat the strike as the source of what follows from it. Present-day disputes over shared water show why fair allocation belongs beside the miracle of supply rather than after it.

---

## Verse 2:61

> And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses! We cannot endure the same meal ˹every day˺. So ˹just˺ call upon your Lord on our behalf, He will bring forth for us some of what the earth produces of herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions.” Moses scolded ˹them˺, “Do you exchange what is better for what is worse? ˹You can˺ go down to any village and you will find what you have asked for.” They were stricken with disgrace and misery, and they invited the displeasure of Allah for rejecting Allah’s signs and unjustly killing the prophets. This is ˹a fair reward˺ for their disobedience and violations

**MANNA REFUSED IN FAVOUR OF ONIONS**

A free supply of food is set aside for the taste of a vegetable stall, and the request is made as though it were reasonable. The people open their case with a complaint about sameness: ***“And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses!”***, ***“We cannot endure the same meal ˹every day˺.”*** The meal they had grown tired of was the manna and the quails, food that arrived without planting, harvest, or market, and it had come to them in a place where nothing grows. Their words are addressed to a prophet rather than to the One who had been feeding them, and the whole request is framed as a favour Moses could do for them if he would only ask. Nothing in the verse suggests hunger; what it reports is weariness with a thing that had never failed. Anyone given a steady good long enough to overlook it will recognise the complaint before its sentence ends, because the complaint is not about the food but about the repetition of it. Ibn ʿAbbās read the better provision as the manna and quails of the wilderness and the lower request as ordinary crops available in settled towns; the rebuke concerns the exchange, not the lawfulness of vegetables.

**THE REQUEST FOR ORDINARY CROPS**

Then the demand is spelled out, and the list is the point: ***“So ˹just˺ call upon your Lord on our behalf, He will bring forth”***, ***“for us some of what the earth produces of herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils”***, ***“and onions.” Moses scolded ˹them˺, “Do you exchange what is better”***. The items named are cheap, common, and heavy: the food of people who work the soil and flavour their bread with what they can buy in the market. Every one of them requires ground to plough, water to carry, and a season to wait through, and the people asking were standing in a desert. The offer they were turning down had no such conditions attached, and they wanted the burden back, since a field they had tilled themselves would feel like their own in a way that falling food never could. The same appetite is described in the earlier chapter of this story, where the people who had been brought out of Egypt ask for the produce they had known there and are answered by the command to go and eat what they please: (2:58 — **“And ˹remember˺ when We said, “Enter this city”**). The earlier verse had offered exactly what they now demanded, freely and on the spot, and they had left it behind.

**A SHORT REBUKE THAT CLOSES THE CASE**

Moses does not argue with the request; he asks a question that exposes it: ***“for what is worse?”***, ***“˹You can˺ go down to any village”***, ***“and you will find what you have asked”***, ***“for.” They were stricken with disgrace”***. The rebuke is short and complete, and its force lies in a comparison the people had not made: what they wanted to trade was better than what they wanted to receive. The permission that follows is not a concession but a sentence, because going down to a village means leaving the arrangement under which they were fed without effort, and the Book has already told the reader what a settled life under a village's economy looks like. A later passage marks how this account was received by generations that came after, when the same community is described as condemned for exactly the pattern of conduct named here: (5:78 — **“The disbelievers among the Children of Israel were condemned in the revelations of David”**). The verse treats the exchange as the beginning of a long descent rather than as an ordinary complaint about food.

**DISGRACE, MISERY, AND THE REASON GIVEN**

The sentence at the end of the request is the heaviest in the verse and each of its parts is named in order: ***“and misery, and they invited the displeasure of Allah”***, ***“for rejecting Allah’s signs”***, ***“and unjustly killing the prophets. This is ˹a fair reward˺”***, ***“for their disobedience and violations”***. Disgrace and misery are attached to a people rather than to an individual, and they are described as something stamped on them, which is how the early teachers explained the words: one glosses the first as a tax laid on them and the second as the dress of poverty, while a later reading notes that a nation stripped of its own rule carries both wherever it settles. The Book then gives the cause, and the cause is not the vegetable request. It is the rejection of signs and the killing of prophets, crimes that had been going on for generations before anyone asked for lentils. The same indictment is repeated elsewhere in the Book with the same two charges joined: (4:155 — **“˹They were condemned˺ for breaking their covenant, rejecting Allah’s signs, killing the prophets unjustly,”**). A reader who stops at the onions will miss what the verse is actually counting.

**THE MECHANISM OF A SLOW REVERSAL**

What the passage shows is that communities do not fall in a single act; they fall by trading a good they have stopped noticing for something smaller they can call their own. The exchange is almost never presented to them as a rejection of God, and in this story it is presented as a menu. The early teachers read this account as a warning about contentment, but the mechanism they describe is broader than taste in food, since the same reversal happens with guidance that has become familiar, prayer that has become routine, and a community that starts measuring its health by what it produces rather than by what it obeys. The Book's answer to such a demand is not a lecture but a permission, and the permission permits exactly the thing desired, which is why it is a punishment. A reader can test the pattern cheaply in his own case by naming the goods he has received without effort and noticing which of them he has begun to describe as boring, since the sentence that follows that discovery is the one this verse was written to interrupt. Today, constant choice can train appetite to despise sound provision merely because it has become familiar.

---

## Verse 2:62

> Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians—whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**WHO IS COUNTED, AND WHAT IS ASKED OF HIM**

The verse widens the field at the moment a reader expects it to narrow: ***“Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians—whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and”***, ***“the Last Day and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And”***, ***“there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve”***. Four communities are named, and the condition that follows cuts across all four of them, since the promise is attached to belief and good conduct rather than to a label. The naming is not a compliment paid to each group; it is a statement that the categories people use to sort themselves are not the categories the reward is sorted by. The Sabians were a small and obscure community in the region, which is exactly why their appearance in the list is significant, since a group with no political weight is included on the same terms as the others. The sentence closes with the two things the Day removes for those who meet its condition, and both are things people carry every day: fear of what is coming, and grief over what is gone. Ibn ʿAbbās applied the promise to those who truly followed Moses and the other prophets, with future fear removed and grief over what had been left behind brought to an end.

**TWO READINGS OF THE WIDENING**

This verse has been read in two ways, and the difference is worth knowing because both readings are held by serious people. One line of reading holds that it describes the position before the final revelation arrived, so that Jews, Christians, and Sabians who lived faithfully within their own dispensations are addressed as a community that has since been replaced by the arrival of the Qur'an. Another line holds that the conditions named remain open to anyone in any time, and that a person who truly believes in God and the Last Day and lives well is not excluded by the name his community carries. The Book itself tests both readings by repeating the list and promise elsewhere, with even the order of the names rearranged: (5:69 — **“Indeed, the believers, Jews, Sabians and Christians—whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and”**). The rearrangement is a small signal that the list is not a ranking. Also carried in the early reports is that the verse came down in answer to a question about the fate of people who had followed earlier prophets, and that the answer described their case rather than abolishing the conditions of belief.

**CREED PROVED THROUGH CONDUCT**

The two beliefs named are joined to a deed, and the deed is not left vague: ***“whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah”*** is placed beside good-doing, so an empty claim, producing nothing in a person's conduct, is not the case the verse is describing. The Last Day is named here as it is named throughout the chapter, because a person's certainty about the meeting shapes what he does with his time and his money. The same combination of faith and good work appears elsewhere in the Book as the one doorway that admits anyone at all: (2:112 — **“But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah”**). The order matters too, since faith comes first and the good deed is its fruit rather than its price; a reader who reverses the order turns the verse into a scheme of payment and loses the mercy it is describing. A second sūrah reports the same principle for the People of the Book individually rather than by group: (3:199 — **“Indeed, there are some among the People of the Book”**). The Book never treats the group as the unit of judgement, even when it addresses people in groups.

**FEAR AND GRIEF, THE TWO THINGS THAT ARE REMOVED**

The last clause is worth a paragraph of its own, because it describes the two things a believer is spared: ***“there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve”***. Fear looks forward and grief looks backward, and between them they consume most of the anxiety a person carries. The reward described here is not a description of gardens, which comes elsewhere in the chapter; it is the removal of the two emotions that make a person unable to enjoy what he has. The early teachers noted that the verse puts the two together because the human being is rarely free of both at once, and that the promise is made in the same breath as the requirement, so that the reader sees them as parts of one arrangement. This is also the place where the comparison with the merchant in the market sits comfortably: a man who has been guaranteed the safety of his goods behind him and a place to sleep ahead of him can trade all day without either of those two weights on his chest.

**ONE CONDITION ACROSS COMMUNITIES**

A reader may finish the verse and ask where the boundary now runs, and the honest answer is that the verse gives the test rather than the roster. The terms it sets are faith in God and in the Last Day, together with good conduct, and it does not add membership of a particular community to the list. That is why communities that read this verse often end up applying it to themselves first, since the conditions are demanding enough to keep anyone busy. The same sūrah returns to the question later with a harder edge, warning that a claim of belonging will not substitute for the work: (98:6 — **“Indeed, those who disbelieve from the People of the Book”**). The verse is therefore best read as an invitation extended before a warning, and as a reminder that the One who will judge on that Day has described in advance what he will be looking at. What remains on the reader's side is to check his own two hands rather than his neighbours' labels, since the promise is written for whoever meets the terms, and no one can answer the terms on another's behalf. In the present day, inherited labels still cannot replace belief that governs conduct when no community audience is watching. The rule is like one gate with several roads approaching it: the road name does not admit anyone who refuses the conditions at the entrance.

---

## Verse 2:63

> And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from you and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.”

**A MOUNTAIN HELD OVER A COVENANT**

The pledge in this verse is taken under a weight that can be seen, and the setting is part of the lesson: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from you”***, ***“and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to”***, ***“that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you”***. A covenant is usually a matter of words, and the Book reports here that words were reinforced by a sight the people could not mistake. The mountain was lifted and held above them, and another sūrah describes the same event with the detail that they thought it would fall on them: (7:171 — **“And ˹remember˺ when We raised the mountain over them”**). What the reader should notice is what the lifted mountain was meant to produce, since it produced agreement rather than conviction, and the Book reports the agreement honestly in a later passage where the same people say they heard and disobeyed. Awe and obedience are two different things, and the verse is careful to show a generation that had the first in abundance while the second was still missing. Ibn ʿAbbās transmitted that the mountain was lifted above the people when the covenant was taken, and that holding firmly meant earnest obedience to the Scripture's permissions, prohibitions, reward and warning.

**SCRIPTURE GRIPPED WITH EARNESTNESS**

The command itself is short, and each part of it deserves its own reading: ***“and observe its teachings”***, ***“so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.””*** The people were told to take hold of what had been given them, which is a stronger image than reading or hearing it, and then to observe what it teaches, which is the working out of that grip in daily conduct. The final clause names the outcome rather than the demand, and the outcome is mindfulness, so the observance is a road to something rather than an end in itself. The same scene appears in a passage that places the lifted mountain beside the command to enter the gate with humility: (4:154 — **“We raised the Mount over them ˹as a warning˺ for ˹breaking˺ their covenant”**). The two accounts together show that this was not a first agreement but a renewal of one already broken, and a renewed pledge taken under a lifted mountain is a measure of how much had already been lost.

**THE SAME PLEDGE UNDER ANOTHER LIGHT**

Readers of this sūrah meet the scene again a few pages on, and the third telling adds the answer the people gave: (2:93 — **“And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺,”**). The repetition is not wasted space; the Book returns to the scene because the community's later conduct has to be measured against the pledge it made at the foot of that mountain. A reader who treats the three tellings as one will hear the agreement as a single event, and the Book's habit of returning to it will look like an editor's duplication rather than an author's insistence. What is being established is a fact about the community's own record, and it is established from more than one direction, which is how the Book treats everything it wants a reader to take seriously.

**WHAT STANDS BEHIND A PLEDGE TAKEN IN FEAR**

There is a plain comparison here with the promises a person makes when he is frightened. A man in a hospital corridor promises a lifetime of worship for one clear scan, and the promise is sincere while the fear lasts; the same man a year later will not be able to recall the exact wording of what he offered. The Book's account of the mountain is a record of that pattern on a national scale, and the mercy in it is that the pledge was still accepted, which is what the next verse says outright. The verse also fixes a principle that runs through the whole chapter: what is taken by awe has to be kept by choice, and the keeping is the part that is tested. A reader who has made promises in a hard season can take the lesson without despair, because the following verse names the door that remains open after the turning away.

**A COVENANT TAKEN AND A COMMAND REPEATED**

What the passage leaves behind is a picture of a people standing under a mountain with a scripture in their hands and a promise on their lips. The words of the command are the same words the reader has been given in this Book, and the outcome named at the end, mindfulness, is the goal the whole sūrah has been working toward since its opening lines. That is why the scene is placed where it is, between the favours and the failures, because it names the thing that was available to that community and to every community after it. The verse does not say the mountain produced obedience; it says the covenant was taken and the command was given, and the reader already knows what happened next. The honest use of the paragraph is therefore not to admire the miracle but to notice how close the command is to the one he carries, and how much of it he has been holding without observing. Today, holding firmly appears in the unglamorous work of keeping a known obligation after the emotion of receiving it has passed.

---

## Verse 2:64

> Yet you turned away afterwards. Had it not been for Allah’s grace and mercy upon you, you would have certainly been of the losers

**A PEOPLE SPARED BY MERCY THEY DID NOT EARN**

The covenant had just been taken, and the verse opens by naming what came next: ***“Yet you turned away afterwards. Had it not been”***, ***“for Allah’s grace and mercy upon you, you would have certainly been of the losers”***. Two sentences, and the second explains why the first did not end the story. The turning away is stated without softening, and the reader is left with a community that broke its word under a lifted mountain and remained on its feet anyway. The reason given is not their repentance, their merit, or their numbers; it is the favour and compassion of the One who took the pledge. The Book returns to this pattern at the end of the very same passage, and the same sentence appears a second time in this sūrah, which tells the reader that the account is being told for the sake of that clause rather than for the sake of the failure. Ibn ʿAbbās read the grace as the deferral of punishment and the mercy as a renewed summons to guidance, which explains why survival after turning away was itself a gift.

**WHAT LOSING WOULD HAVE MEANT**

The word chosen for the outcome is worth stopping over, because the Book uses it for a specific kind of ruin. A person who is lost in this vocabulary is not merely punished; he has thrown away his own share, which is the sense the term carries elsewhere when covenant-breakers are described in the opening of the sūrah. Earlier in this chapter the same word is used of those who violate the pledge after affirming it: (2:27 — **“those who violate Allah’s covenant after it has been affirmed,”**). The community in the verse was on the road to exactly that description, and the sentence that saves them is a sentence about God rather than about them. A reader who notices this will see that the verse is not describing a light offence. It is describing a fall that was prevented by a hand that was not the people's own, and the prevention is the mercy named.

**MERCY THAT DOES NOT WAIT FOR REPENTANCE**

The reports and the rest of the Book agree on one point here that is easy to miss: the favour is described as already upon them, not as conditional on anything they had done. Another sūrah makes the principle general and puts it in the mouth of the revelation addressed to a people whose record matches this one: (7:153 — **“But those who commit evil, then repent and become ˹true˺ believers,”**). The door described there is open after the evil, which is the same order of events as this verse: failure first, mercy second. A third passage states the invitation in the widest terms available in the Book: (39:53 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet, that Allah says,˺ “O My servants”**). Read together, the three passages give the reader a settled picture: the Book never treats a broken pledge as the end of a person's case, and it never treats mercy as a licence to break the next one.

**SPARED DOES NOT YET MEAN SAFE**

A second point follows from the wording, and it belongs to the reader's own life rather than to the history. Being spared is not the same as being safe, since the people in this verse were kept alive and kept in the story while the pattern of their conduct was already visible. The Book tells the reader that the covenant was broken and the mercy came, and then it goes on in the next verses to describe what a later generation of the same people did with the Sabbath. A reader who takes the mercy as a verdict on the future will be surprised by the next page, and the one who takes it as an opening will use it, which is the difference the clause is meant to make. This is the chapter's constant method: it shows the kindness of God beside the conduct of man, and it refuses to let either of the two cancel the other.

**TURNING BACK AFTER TURNING AWAY**

The verse has an application that is worth stating plainly, and it concerns the shape of repentance rather than its sincerity. A person who has broken a promise and is still walking around has already received a favour he did not arrange, and the appropriate response is not a fresh vow spoken in fear but a change of course performed in calm. The same sūrah closes with a prayer the community is taught to make about exactly this: being spared the burden of what one has already done and helped toward what comes next. A reader with a broken covenant behind him can take two things from the verse: that his story is still running, and that the mercy which kept him standing through the failure is the same mercy whose standard will measure what he does with the time it bought, so the leniency is also a summons. Present-day reprieve is often mistaken for approval, although delayed consequences may instead be space in which return is still possible. It follows that grace is not merely an inward comfort here; it is the only barrier between a turned back and an irreversible loss.

---

## Verse 2:65

> You are already aware of those of you who broke the Sabbath. We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!”

**THE TOWN THAT WORKED THE SABBATH**

The next failure is presented as something the reader already knows about: ***“You are already aware of those of you”***, ***“who broke the Sabbath. We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!””*** The phrase assumes knowledge, and the rest of the Book supplies it. A coastal settlement was tested with a day of rest, the fish came to the surface on the day they were forbidden to fish, and they went after them anyway. The account is given in another sūrah with the scene laid out: (7:163 — **“Ask them ˹O Prophet˺ about ˹the people of˺ the town”**). What the Book reports here is the outcome rather than the method, and the outcome is not a fine or a delay. It is a change of what the offenders were. Ibn ʿAbbās located the Sabbath breach in the age of David and took the command as a real abasement, not merely a comparison used to insult the offenders.

**A PUNISHMENT THAT IS REPORTED AS A CHANGE OF NATURE**

The words used are the strongest in the passage, and the Book repeats them in a second place where the sequence is clearer: (7:166 — **“But when they stubbornly persisted in violation, We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!””**). The repetition matters because it removes the possibility that the sentence was a figure of speech used once for effect. The same fate is recalled again in a later sūrah among the people who earned a punishment worse than the ones they mocked: (5:60 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Shall I inform you of those”**). The early teachers differed over whether the transformation was physical or whether it described a moral descent, and the difference is a real one; what no reader of the verse can miss is that the Book chose a form of punishment that took away the offenders' standing as people among whom a conversation could be held.

**EVADING THE LETTER AND BREAKING THE PURPOSE**

The town's failure is worth examining because it was not a simple refusal. They had found a way to keep the form of the Sabbath while taking its fruit, and the Book's naming of the day as broken rather than ignored is precise. A later chapter describes the mechanics with the fish appearing on the forbidden day and vanishing on the permitted one, which shows a test designed to expose what was already in them. Nothing in the account suggests that they doubted the command; they arranged their lives around it in order to defeat it. The same instinct appears in this sūrah among people who alter words they were told to say, and it appears among the traders of any century who keep a rule's wording while dismantling its purpose. The verse therefore belongs beside the account of the changed words, since both are stories about obedience that has been hollowed out from the inside.

**ALREADY KNOWN BEFORE IT IS TOLD**

The opening clause tells the reader something about how this book teaches, since it treats the incident as established before it is mentioned. That is the way a community's own history works: it is carried in the memory of the people and referred to rather than introduced. The Qur'an uses the same method with the events of Badr and the accounts of earlier prophets, and it does so because the point of the retelling is never the news. What is new in this verse is the sentence that was spoken, and the sentence is quoted to deliver the verdict in its own words. A reader who has been given the story elsewhere is expected to bring it with him, and the Book trusts him to do so.

**THE COST OF A CLEVER EVASION**

The lasting value of the passage for a reader is that it shows where a clever evasion ends if it is left to run. The people in the town did not hold a debate about the Sabbath; they went fishing on the day the fishing was forbidden, and they would have told anyone who asked that the sea was theirs. A small community with a small rule broke it in a small way, and the punishment removed them from the human conversation altogether. That is why the next verse says their fate was made an example, and why the Book puts the story in front of a community that has been given a much larger trust. The reader who wants to test himself on it can begin with the rules he has quietly learned to satisfy in form while ignoring in substance, since that is the list the people of the coast were working from when the fish appeared on the wrong day of the week. Today, clever compliance that empties a rule of its purpose remains a breach even when every movement has been arranged to look legal.

---

## Verse 2:66

> So We made their fate an example to present and future generations, and a lesson to the God-fearing

**THE SABBATH BREACH LEFT AS A MARKER**

The fate of the Sabbath-breakers is turned outward in this verse, and that is the whole of its work: ***“So We made their fate an example to present”***, ***“and future generations, and a lesson to the God-fearing”***. The word behind the translation "example" is not the ordinary word for a sign; it carries the sense of a punishment that is displayed so that others will be deterred by it and go another way. Two audiences are named, and the two are not the same kind of people. The generations are those who will hear about it later, and the God-fearing are those who will take the warning seriously, which the Book names because a warning does nothing for a reader who has already decided that it is not addressed to him. The verse therefore says something that many readers would rather not hear: a punishment can serve a purpose beyond the offender, and the Book is telling the reader plainly that this one does. Ibn ʿAbbās read the event as a warning to later people not to repeat the same breach and as counsel that especially profits those already disposed to fear God.

**WHO PROFITS FROM THE OLD ACCOUNT**

The closing clause identifies the people who profit from the incident, and the identification is worth pausing over. A person who already fears God hears the story and finds in it a reason to keep to the command, and the same account leaves a careless reader with nothing but an item of history. This is the difference the Book keeps drawing between the two ways of reading a warning: the one who obeys before he is caught and the one who learns only from consequences. The same sūrah uses the same logic when it warns its readers of a fate that would be worse than the one described here, in the way their faces could be turned backwards and the people behind the warning stand as a precedent: (4:47 — **“O you who were given the Book! Believe in what We have revealed—confirming”**). The verse records a punishment that has already been paid by others precisely so that a later reader does not have to pay it himself.

**THE EXAMPLE AS PUBLIC HISTORY**

The Book's habit of turning events into public history deserves its own note here, because it explains why the story was placed in the middle of this chapter rather than in a chronicle. A community remembers what it is told to remember, and the Book tells it to remember this, which is why the verse assumes the reader has heard the account before it is repeated; the same assumption appears in another passage where the audience is told to ask about the town by the sea, which is the same story twice removed. The effect of retelling is that the offence is stripped of its particulars, since the fish and the day are left behind and what remains is a settled rule about what happens to people who arrange their lives around breaking a command. The reader receives a case with a verdict in it, and the verdict is meant to be carried rather than stored.

**KNOWING AN ACCOUNT AND PROFITING FROM IT**

There is a real gap between hearing an account and taking a lesson from it, and the verse names that gap when it says the lesson belongs to the God-fearing. The reader can test the difference in his own house, since the same story about a family's money that one son treats as a warning another treats as a joke, and the story is not the variable. What the Book calls fear of God is not a mood; it is the settled condition of a person who expects to be held to what he knows, and it is the soil a warning needs in order to produce anything. That is why the verse puts the account of the coast behind it and then refuses to promise that everyone who hears will improve, since the promise is made to a quality of reader rather than to a quantity of information.

**TURNING AN ACCOUNT INTO A DECISION**

A warning that is never applied becomes a story, and the Book's closing clause tells the reader which of the two he should aim for. The practical effect of the verse is that the punishment is no longer only about the people of the town; it is described as standing in front of later generations, which includes anyone reading the page. The reader who takes the account seriously will look at the rules he has learned to satisfy in form, since that was the offence, and will treat a small deliberate breach as the beginning of a longer road rather than as an exception. The verse ends on the God-fearing, and in doing so it quietly asks the reader which of the two companies he is standing in. In the present day, public memory serves its purpose only when an old collapse changes the next decision under similar pressure. It is like a warning marker beside a collapsed bridge, useful only to travellers who let the earlier ruin change their route.

---

## Verse 2:67

> And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow.” They replied, “Are you mocking us?” Moses responded, “I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!”

**A COMMAND OF SACRIFICE MEETS A SHRUG**

The chapter takes its name from the animal in this verse, and the exchange that follows is one of the strangest in the Book: ***“And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow.” They replied, “Are you mocking us?””***, ***“Moses responded, “I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!””*** The command is delivered in the plainest words a prophet can use, and the answer he receives questions his seriousness rather than the command's content. The people had lived through the sea, the water from the rock, the shade, and the food that fell from the sky, and their first reaction to an instruction is the suspicion that their prophet is playing with them. Moses' reply is worth more attention than it usually receives, because he does not say that God does not jest; he says that he takes refuge from being counted among the foolish, which is a different and sharper answer. Ibn ʿAbbās understood the first command to permit any cow; the narrowing came only after the people treated a plain order as mockery and continued to ask.

**MOCKERY WOULD BETRAY THE PROPHETIC OFFICE**

The word Moses uses of himself describes a person who does not know what he is doing or a person whose conduct has no weight in it. Accusing a prophet of mockery is a charge against his office, and the reply turns the charge back in the only direction that preserves the office: a man who invents commands on his own authority is exactly the kind of person who should not be believed. The early teachers noted that this is the first thing Moses says in the exchange, before any explanation of the command is offered, because the question he is answering is about him and not about the cow. The Book's own usage of the word elsewhere puts the same weight on it, and the reader can hear the register in a passage where the accusation of folly is what a prophet's opponents throw at each other: (7:66 — **“The disbelieving chiefs of his people responded, “We surely see you as a fool,”**). Moses' sentence, read in that light, is a refusal to be sorted into the class of people whose words can be dismissed.

**A QUESTION ASKED OUT OF HABIT**

The reader of this chapter already knows that the people's questions are not innocent. They had asked for a visible god, they had asked for the vegetables of Egypt, and each time the asking had been a step away from what they had been given. The request for detail in the verses that follow has an obvious practical cause, since the command did not name any particular animal, and a general command invites a question about which of many possible animals is meant. What turns the question into a fault is the manner of it, and the Book's guidance for a later community addresses that manner directly, since it warns against the questions that make a clarified command heavier: (2:108 — **“Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger”**). The people wanted the command made easier by being made narrower, and every clarification they obtained made the animal harder to find, which is the pattern the next three verses describe.

**THE COW, THE MURDER, AND THE REASON FOR BOTH**

The name of this sūrah comes from the animal, and the animal is connected to a death that the chapter reports a few verses later. A man had been killed, the killer was unknown, and the community disputed the matter until the Book told them to strike the body with part of the cow that had been slaughtered. The command, then, was never only a test of willingness; it was the preparation for a sign that would expose what the community was hiding. A reader who takes the two passages together sees why the sacrifice is placed first: an argument about which cow is to be killed delays an answer to a murder, and the delay belongs to the people rather than to the command. The same willingness is asked of a later community in the same book, in a passage that warns against the questions that make a clarified command heavier: (5:101 — **“may disturb you.”**). A general instruction is a mercy, and the insistence on detail is what turns it into a burden.

**PLAIN DUTY AND PROTECTIVE REFUGE**

Two things stand out for a person reading the passage on his own. The first concerns the tone in which a command is met, since the people's suspicion was a judgement passed on their prophet before the command was even considered, and the same instinct survives wherever a clear instruction arrives and the first question is about the messenger's motives. The second concerns the way Moses answers, because he neither defends the command nor asks for an apology; he puts himself in the position of a man who takes God's orders seriously and leaves the accusation where it belongs. A reader who has been given a plain duty and found himself asking for the details to be settled before he begins can see the shape of his own exchange in this one. The verse closes with the prophet's refuge taken from folly, and it invites the reader to take his own. Today, a plain duty can still be delayed by questioning the speaker's tone instead of meeting the substance of what was asked. The exchange is like a worker receiving a clear assignment and answering by asking whether the supervisor is joking.

---

## Verse 2:68

> They said, “Call upon your Lord to clarify for us what type ˹of cow˺ it should be!” He replied, “Allah says, ‘The cow should neither be old nor young but in between. So do as you are commanded!’”

**QUESTIONS THAT NARROWED A SIMPLE ORDER**

The first answer to the first request does not describe an unusual animal; it describes an ordinary one and adds a rebuke at the end: ***“They said, “Call upon your Lord to clarify”***, ***“for us what type ˹of cow˺ it should be!””***, ***“He replied, “Allah says, ‘The cow should neither be old nor young”***, ***“but in between. So do”***, ***“as you are commanded!’””*** The age given excludes the two extremes and leaves the middle, which is where most cows of a herd are found, so the answer had closed the question rather than opened it. What follows is the sentence the people should have heard first, because it tells them that the command had been sufficient as it stood and that the asking was the problem. The report carried from Ibn ʿAbbās states that any cow would have been enough, so the whole description came from the questioners themselves rather than from the command. The Book records their questions and the answers that narrowed the choice, and the record is a lesson in how a simple duty becomes a difficult one.

**AN ANSWER THAT KEPT NARROWING THE FIELD**

Each clarification that follows removes more animals from the field, and the pattern is deliberate rather than accidental. The older accounts agree that the people's insistence on detail is what made the detail binding, since the command had been left open as a mercy and they pressed for a specification. The same principle runs through the Book's treatment of the Sabbath in the account of the town by the sea, where a prohibition was turned into a puzzle and then into a punishment. A reader who has watched a committee take a clear instruction and return it twice for elaboration will recognise the process, and the cost of elaboration is that the original freedom is gone. Nothing in the passage suggests that the people were confused; they were unwilling, and the questions are the shape their unwillingness took.

**THE ONE THING THEY WERE TOLD TO DO**

The clause that ends the verse is worth carrying out of the passage, since it is the Book's own summary of the exchange: they were told to act on what they had already been given. The command had been to sacrifice a cow, and nothing in the first instruction required a description of the animal's age; the people, however, had learned to treat a general command as an incomplete one. Their habit had a history, since the same generation had asked for a visible god while Moses was on the mountain, and had turned to a calf when the wait grew long: (7:148 — **“In the absence of Moses,”**). A community that asks for detail in order to postpone obedience will find that the detail arrives, that it is heavier than the original, and that the delay has made the duty harder to perform than it was at the start.

**WHEN CLARIFICATION BECOMES DELAY**

The practical application of this verse is uncomfortable, because the instinct it exposes is not confined to that people. A person who is told to give in charity and asks which charity, in what amount, and by when, has begun the same conversation, and the outcomes are the same: an obligation that could have been discharged in an afternoon sits undone while its terms are negotiated. The Book's answer here is not that questions are forbidden; a genuine difficulty can be raised and answered. What is exposed is the use of a question as a place to stand still, and the remedy is the one sentence in the verse that the people never took up. A reader who has a plain duty waiting on his desk and a list of clarifications he intended to request can test this verse against his own week, and he will usually find that the duty was clear enough from the beginning.

**EACH SPECIFICATION ADDED WEIGHT**

The verse leaves a reader with a rule about how guidance works in practice: it is given in a form he can carry, and if he insists on unpacking it before he moves, the unpacking becomes part of what he has to carry. The Book's method in this passage is to let the people's own questions produce their difficulty, so that no reader can blame the command for the weight. A second thing to notice is that the answer never withdraws the command or expresses regret at having given it; the duty remains, and the animal described in the next verses can still be found. That is the mercy hidden inside the narrowing, since the door stayed open even after the terms had grown tight. The reader who wants something to do rather than something to discuss can begin with the next verse's colour and see for himself how much narrower the field has become. Present-day forms and approval chains can likewise turn a simple task into an expensive maze when questions are used to postpone action. It is like turning a request for a chair into a search for one exact tree, colour and workshop until the simple need becomes costly.

---

## Verse 2:69

> They said, “Call upon your Lord to specify for us its colour.” He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should be a bright yellow cow—pleasant to see.’”

**A COLOUR GIVEN AND A FIELD NARROWED AGAIN**

The second request is about appearance, and the answer this time is a description that can be seen from a distance: ***“They said, “Call upon your Lord to specify”***, ***“for us its colour.” He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should be a bright yellow cow”***, ***“pleasant to see.’””*** The animal is now middle-aged and unmistakably coloured, and the questions have removed two large classes of cattle from the herd in two verses. What the verse adds to the description is the effect the colour has on the people who look at it, and that detail is not decoration; it tells the reader that the animal would be recognisable on sight, which makes the search a matter of looking rather than of guessing. An early report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās describes the shade as the deepest yellow, the kind that draws the eye of anyone who sees it, and the Book's own phrasing leaves the beholder inside the sentence. A command that had been answered with one word now describes a specimen.

**WHO ASKED FOR THE DETAILS, AND WHAT THEY COST**

The people had asked for the colour, so the colour is supplied, and this is the second occasion on which their question shaped the obligation. There is a pattern here that readers of the chapter have noticed for centuries: the more precise the answer, the fewer the animals that qualify, and by the end of the exchange the descriptions add up to a creature so specific that its owner had to be sought out. The reports that came down about this search say that the animal was eventually found in the keeping of a young man, and that he named a price which the people paid. A reader may take that report or leave it, but the arithmetic of the command is in the Book itself and needs no report: three questions, three specifications, and a herd of thousands reduced to one. The questions were answered generously, which is exactly why they became costly.

**THE OLD CALF THAT THEY HAD MADE**

The colour in this verse is also the chapter's quietest reminder of a failure that came earlier in the same history. While Moses was on the mountain, the people had made an idol from their ornaments and called it their god, and the Book describes that image as a calf: (20:88 — **“Then he moulded for them an idol of a calf”**). A community that had once asked for a golden calf to worship is now being asked for a yellow cow to offer, and the parallel is difficult to miss. The similarity is in the eye rather than in the substance, since one was an object of worship and the other an animal of sacrifice, while the opposing purposes of the acts separate worship from obedient sacrifice. The Book places the two close enough for a reader to feel the correction: the wealth of Egypt taken as jewellery had once been melted into a god, and it is now spent on an offering to the God who had brought them out.

**NEGOTIATION PRICED AT ITS TRUE COST**

A person who is used to quick transactions will find the sequence in these verses familiar in a way that is not flattering. Think of a man who asks a builder for a quote, then asks for a second option, then a third, and finds at the end that the work costs more and the season is gone. The people of this story did the same with a command of God, and the last verse of the exchange reports what it did to them: they said the truth had come at last, and they killed the animal without conviction. The specification that made the search hard was their own work, and the Book lets the reader feel the weight of the search before it says so. What a reader should take from the colour is that the answer to a request is not always a gift; sometimes it is the request itself, returned to the asker with its price attached.

**A SPECIFICATION AND A SAINT'S RELUCTANCE**

The verse ends with an animal that can be identified and a duty that can be discharged, so its lesson is not the impossibility of obedience. The lesson is that the field of options narrows with every negotiation, and that the people who negotiate are usually the last to notice the cost of the narrowing. A reader who has a task in front of him and a habit of asking for more clarity should hear the third question coming, because it arrives in the next verse with a complaint about how much alike cows look. The colour given here was a mercy on its own terms, since a bright yellow animal is not hard to find; it became a burden only when the people treated the finding as a puzzle instead of a task. The instruction at the end of the previous verse is still waiting to be carried out, and no further information is going to make it easier. Today, an attractive detail can occupy so much attention that the duty for which the detail was supplied nearly disappears. The effect of the colour is therefore practical as well as visual, because each answer removes another excuse for postponement.

---

## Verse 2:70

> Again they said, “Call upon your Lord so that He may make clear to us which cow, for all cows look the same to us. Then, Allah willing, we will be guided ˹to the right one˺.”

**LATE DEPENDENCE AFTER REPEATED DELAY**

The same request is made a third time, and this time it carries an admission: ***“Again they said, “Call upon your Lord”***, ***“so that He may make clear to us”***, ***“which cow, for all cows look the same to us.”***, ***“Then, Allah willing, we will be guided ˹to the right one˺.””*** After two specifications they still do not know what they are looking for, and they say so, and the sentence shows what the earlier questions had done to them. There is a word in the third clause that stands out, because the phrase acknowledging God's will appears here for the first time in the whole exchange, and it appears after the demands rather than before them.
