The promise to be guided is made at the end of a request for more information, and the order of the two says something about the state of the people asking. The Book reports their words as they were spoken, and the reader who has negotiated with a clear duty will hear the tone. Ibn ʿAbbās read the request as a demand to know whether the animal worked the soil, and he connected the late appeal to God's will with eventual guidance to its exact description.

**WHY ALL COWS HAD COME TO LOOK ALIKE**

The complaint is true, and that is what makes it instructive: two specifications had turned the herd into a puzzle. A reader who wants to see how the narrowing works can take the arithmetic himself, since an age range removes the old and the young, a colour removes every other shade, and what is left is a crowd of animals that differ in ways the questioners had not thought to ask about. The reports from the early teachers describe this state of affairs plainly, and one of them notes that the people had made their own task hard when a single cow of any description would have satisfied the command. The same pattern is visible in the account of the golden calf, where the people who could not wait for a prophet found an image to follow that led them nowhere: (7:148 — **“his people made from their ˹golden˺ jewellery an idol of a calf”**). A community that keeps asking for signs ends up unable to read the ones in front of it.

**THE PLACE OF IF GOD WILLS IN A PROMISE**

The clause about God's will is the one hopeful element in the verse, and its position is the lesson. A person who says that he will act, God willing, has placed his intention under the knowledge of the One who knows whether it will happen, and the words carry no credit unless they shape the conduct that follows. Here they come after three requests for clarification, which is late, and the reader can see the difference between a phrase used to cover a delay and a phrase used to hand one's plans over. The same community is described elsewhere in the chapter as having said that it heard and then disobeyed, and the gap between the saying and the doing is the chapter's recurring subject. What makes the clause in this verse worth noticing is that the promise was kept, since the animal was finally killed, and the Book records both the hesitation and the outcome.

**A PERSON WHO ASKS FOR ONE MORE DETAIL**

The application is easy to see, because the pattern does not require a herd or a prophet. Think of a man who will begin praying once he has arranged his day properly, and then once he has bought the right mat, and then once he has learned the correct words, and who finds after a year that the days are as disordered as they were and the mat is still unused. Each request is reasonable and each answer removes an excuse, and the result is a person who knows more about prayer and does less of it. The Book's account of the cow is the classic description of that temperament, and the people in it are not portrayed as stupid; they are portrayed as unwilling and inventive. A reader who recognises himself in the third question can do the one thing the questioners eventually did, which was to stop asking and act on what they already had.

**AN OBJECTION THAT CORRECTS ITSELF**

The verse is unusual because the people correct themselves inside the sentence they use to delay, and both halves of their state remain visible: the demand for more clarity and the admission that they will need God's help to reach the animal. That combination is closer to the human condition than either half alone, and it is why the passage has been read as a description of hesitation rather than of unbelief. The next verse supplies the last of the specifications and the people's response to it, and the response shows what the hesitation was worth in the end. For a reader, the useful thing in this page is the moment he notices that his own questions are also a form of speech addressed to God, and that they will be answered in a way that leaves him with the duty he started with. In the present day, repeated requests for certainty can become a respectable disguise for unwillingness to begin.

---

## Verse 2:71

> He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should have been used neither to till the soil nor water the fields; wholesome and without blemish.’” They said, “Now you have come with the truth.” Yet they still slaughtered it hesitantly

**THE LAST DESCRIPTION AND THE RELUCTANT KNIFE**

The final answer closes the specification with a working life rather than a colour: ***“He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should have been used neither to till the soil”***, ***“nor water the fields”***, ***“wholesome and without blemish.’” They said, “Now you have come with the truth.””***, ***“Yet they still slaughtered it hesitantly”***. An animal that has never been yoked is one whose whole life has been kept for something else, and an animal without a mark on it is one that nobody could have confused with another. Every question has now been answered, the search has a single answer, and the people acknowledge it in words that sound like belief. The final sentence then reports what the words were worth, and it is the Book's most exact description of the gap between agreement and obedience. They had run out of questions and still went to the animal without conviction. Ibn ʿAbbās understood the final marks to exclude an animal broken by field labour or carrying water and to require one free of blemish and coloured spots.

**A LIFE THAT HAD BEEN KEPT FOR THIS**

The description of the cow as one that never pulled a plough or carried water is worth reading twice, because it is the only specification that has nothing to do with the animal's body. A beast of that kind had been spared the ordinary use of a farm animal for its whole life, and whatever reasons the owners had for sparing it, the effect was that an unspent life was available on the day the command arrived. The reports say the animal was finally found with a young man who named a price for it, and that the community paid what he asked. A reader who wants a comparison can think of the tools and the hours that were kept aside in his own house for a purpose he never quite began, since the animal in this verse is the reverse of that picture: something preserved without knowing why, and used at last for the reason it was preserved.

**THE TRUTH ACKNOWLEDGED AND THE HAND HELD BACK**

The words they speak are a real admission, and the Book does not treat them as empty; the truth had come and they said so. What follows the admission is the point of the verse, because hesitation is a decision that has not been made and a knife that has not fallen, and the animal's blood was shed in the end by people who had argued their way to the edge of obedience. The same hesitation is described in the Book where the people are reported to have said that they heard and then disobeyed, and where the delay in another command became a test of its own kind: (2:93 — **““Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and obey,” they answered,”**). The verse therefore completes the exchange with an accurate verdict: they did the thing, and they did it without the willingness that would have made it worship.

**EXCHANGE NARROWED TO ONE ANIMAL**

Taken from the first command to the last reluctant cut, the passage is one arc, and the arc ends with a duty performed and a lesson left over. The lesson is not about cattle; it is about what happens when a person receives an instruction and treats it as a subject for discussion. The people of this story were not asked to do something impossible, and the animal they finally found was not rare until they had made it rare. When they had exhausted their questions they did what they had been told at the beginning, which means the delay cost them time, money, and the willingness that the duty had been designed to test. A reader who wants to apply this needs nothing more than the last sentence, because it names the moment at which he can stop asking and start acting.

**A SLOW HAND AND A CLOSED FILE**

Broadcasters and editors know the kind of person who will agree to a fact and then decline to broadcast it, and the Book's portrait here is the same figure in a religious key. The reader can check the pattern in his own life by naming one duty he has already accepted with his mind and has not yet done with his hands. The Book treats that gap as the real subject of the exchange, and it attaches a single word to the people involved that a reader can carry away: they were near to not doing it. The mercy in the passage is that the command was carried out at last, so the story is not a warning about lost causes; it is a description of the ordinary way human beings arrive at obedience, late and unenthusiastic. The verse closes the file on the cow, and the next page turns to a killing that the community had been hiding. Today, a person may finally possess every specification and still hesitate because information was never the true obstacle.

---

## Verse 2:72

> ˹This is˺ when a man was killed and you disputed who the killer was, but Allah revealed what you concealed

**A KILLING, A DISPUTE, AND WHAT WAS HIDDEN**

The verse that explains the cow arrives at last, and it is a murder case: ***“˹This is˺ when a man was killed”***, ***“and you disputed who the killer was”***, ***“but Allah revealed what you concealed”***. The community had been told to slaughter an animal, and the reason is a body and an argument. The Book does not say who the dead man was, and it does not say how he died; it says that a killing happened and that the people fell to disputing about it, which is the way of a group that has something to protect. The dispute is the second act of concealment in the verse, since the arguing itself is described as the cover under which the truth was kept. The last clause names the outcome without describing the method, and the method is supplied by the next verse, where a piece of the cow is used to raise the dead man so that he can name his killer. Ibn ʿAbbās described the concealed matter as the identity of a killer over whom the people had quarrelled, so the dispute was not lack of evidence alone but an effort to bury responsibility. The command to truthful justice elsewhere supplies the rule the concealed killer violated: (4:135 — **“stand firm for justice as witnesses for Allah even if it is against yourselves”**).

**A GROUP THAT PREFERS THE ARGUMENT**

The scene is worth reading as a description of how a group handles a crime inside itself. A killing among a people who share a town usually produces two responses: the innocent demand an inquiry, and whoever is implicated begins to move the discussion toward accusations that cannot be settled. The Book reports the second response and says nothing about an inquiry, which tells the reader that the community had chosen the argument over the search. The law given to this people would later require the finding of a body and the swearing of oaths when the killer was unknown, and the chapter's own account of that arrangement comes much later in the sūrah. What is happening here is the failure that arrangement was built to prevent: a group so concerned with where blame would land that it stopped asking what had actually happened.

**ALLAH REVEALING WHAT THEY HAD COVERED**

The clause at the end is the Book's own comment on concealment, and it carries the promise that nothing hidden in this matter will stay hidden. The same subject is taken up later in the chapter, where the readers are told that God knows what they conceal and what they reveal, and the theme is one of the threads that runs through the whole section on this people. Here the hidden thing is disclosed by an act that no one could have planned: a dead man speaking after being struck with part of a sacrifice. The old reports say the community had tried to avoid the consequences of the killing by arguing about it, and the answer they received exposed the killer without naming him in advance. A reader who has watched an institution handle a failure by managing the discussion will see the same instinct in this verse, and the same certainty that it cannot finally work.

**THE PIECE OF A COW AND THE STRIKE**

The instruction in the next verse is the reason the cow was required, and the sequence makes the delay in the earlier passage visible: while the people were asking about the animal's age and colour, a dead man was waiting to be named. A reader can measure the cost of the delay by that fact alone, because every question they asked postponed the answer to a murder that was sitting in their town. The accounts handed down describe the animal being struck and the dead man rising, and some add that he told those present who had killed him and then died again. Whether or not the reader follows those details, the structure of the lesson stands on its own: the Book used a sacrifice to expose a killing, and the people who had been quarrelling about the crime had to watch it become public.

**A HIDDEN DEATH AND ITS CONSEQUENCES**

There is an application here that a reader in any community can use, and it concerns the moment when a group stops investigating and starts blaming. The people in this story had a body, they had a dispute, and they had the means to find out the truth in the demand to sacrifice the animal, and they spent their time on the terms. That is not a failure of knowledge; it is a failure of willingness, and the passage presents it as such by letting the truth arrive anyway. A reader who has seen a family quarrel over an inheritance that was always going to be divided, or a workplace argue over a fault while the fault continued, has seen this verse play out. The Book ends the account by naming what God does with what people bury, and it leaves the reader to decide where he would rather stand when the uncovering happens. Present-day investigations meet the same human impulse when competing stories are used to keep an inconvenient fact from the record. The dispute is like several hands pushing a file across a table so that no fingerprint appears to own it.

---

## Verse 2:73

> So We instructed, “Strike the dead body with a piece of the cow.” This is how ˹easily˺ Allah brings the dead to life, showing you His signs so that you may understand

**A STRIKE THAT PUT THE DEAD BACK ON HIS FEET**

The instruction is delivered and the miracle follows it in one sentence: ***“So We instructed, “Strike the dead body with a piece of the cow.” This is how ˹easily˺ Allah brings the dead to life, showing you His signs”***, ***“so that you may understand”***. Nothing is said about the moment life returned, and the words of the dead man are left out. The verse states what the act was for, which is the point the reader is meant to keep: the sign was given so that the people could understand something about the One who gives life. The command to strike is itself instructive, since the instrument of resurrection is a piece of an animal that had been slaughtered in obedience, and the miracle is tied to an act of compliance that had cost the community an argument. What they had haggled over for days became the means by which a dead man spoke. Ibn ʿAbbās transmitted several views about which part of the cow touched the body, but kept the settled point in front: the revival was a sign of resurrection and a summons to understand it. A later denier voices the very doubt this revival answers: (36:78 — **“And they argue with Us—forgetting they were created—saying, “Who will give life to decayed bones?””**).

**THE SIGN THAT SETTLED A CASE**

The first purpose of the miracle was local and practical: a murder had to be resolved and the Book says earlier that the truth had been concealed. The second purpose is named in this verse and is much larger, since the raising of one man was a demonstration of the power that will raise everyone. The Book often uses a particular event to carry a general truth, and this is one of its clearest cases, because the same verb that describes the dead man standing up describes what will happen to all the dead on the day of the meeting. A reader who wants to hold the two together can read the verse as an advance instalment of an event that the whole sūrah has been building toward since its opening description of the believers and their certainty about the meeting. The crowd watching that day saw one man; the readers of the page are meant to see the whole promise.

**THE DETAILS THE ACCOUNTS ADD**

The accounts that came down about this scene add details that the verse leaves out, and the reader may take them as reports rather than as the text itself. They describe the animal being struck, the dead man rising, and the naming of the killer; some add that he asked to be returned, and one tradition says the sign was given to a single man so that a community's quarrel could end. The verse itself is spare by comparison with those accounts, which is a reminder that the Book's telling is arranged for the reader's benefit rather than for the sake of the story. The same power is described in another passage of this sūrah in exactly those terms, where the raising of the dead is placed beside the other signs given to earlier prophets. What a reader can check for himself is the connection the verse itself makes, since it moves from one raised body to the general power in a single sentence.

**AN IMAGE FROM AN ORDINARY WEEK**

The image here is easy to carry into a common experience, because everyone has watched a situation that seemed finished come back to life. A case that was closed, a debt that was written off, a friendship that had been given up for lost: the return of any of them is unexpected in the same way as a dead man standing up, though the power behind it is rarely noticed. The Book's use of the smaller event to teach the larger one is the same method a teacher uses when he points at a lamp and speaks of the sun. What the sign was designed to correct in the people watching it was not a doubt about their own resurrection; it was the habit of treating God's commands as negotiable business. A reader who finds his own attention slipping during an argument over details may be the person this verse was written for.

**UNDERSTANDING AS THE PURPOSE OF A SIGN**

The verse ends with the word for understanding, which places the miracle in the service of a mind that has to be changed rather than a crowd that has to be impressed. Signs in the Book are regularly followed by this same clause, and the clause makes the reader responsible for what he does with what he has seen. A miracle that produces no change of conduct has missed the purpose named here, and the people in this story had already seen enough wonders to fill a lifetime. The demand for proofs and the failure to draw conclusions from them are both present in the chapter, sometimes in the same paragraph about the same people. The verse therefore closes the account of the cow with the reason it was all arranged, and the reason is not the animal at all: it is that a community should come to understand what it had been watching. Today, the verse corrects the assumption that life can be measured only by mechanisms already familiar to human observation.

---

## Verse 2:74

> Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder, for some rocks gush rivers; others split, spilling water; while others are humbled in awe of Allah. And Allah is never unaware of what you do

**A HEART HARDER THAN THE STONE IT SAW**

The sign has been given and the chapter turns immediately to the state of the people who received it: ***“Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock”***, ***“or even harder, for some rocks gush rivers”***, ***“others split, spilling water”***, ***“while others are humbled in awe of Allah.”***, ***“And Allah is never unaware of what you do”***. The comparison is not between a heart and any stone, but between a heart and the stones that do something, since the verse names the rocks that give water and the rocks that fall in awe and leaves the hardened heart with neither of those capacities. That is the force of the phrase about being harder: a stone can be softer than a heart if the stone responds to its Lord and the heart does not. The reader who watched water come out of stone earlier in this sūrah is now asked to compare the rock's obedience with the people's, since the same event is retold with the command that produced it: (2:60 — **“And ˹remember˺ when Moses prayed for water for his people, We said, “Strike the rock with your staff.””**). Ibn ʿAbbās connected the hardening to the refusal that followed even after the victim had been revived and his killer disclosed; a witnessed sign had not produced submission.

**WHY STONE BECOMES THE COMPARISON**

The choice of comparison is deliberate, because the community had just watched a stone produce twelve streams at the command of God. Any stone in that history was a better servant than the hearts that had watched the miracle and gone on as before, and the verse says so without softening the language. The same image is used elsewhere in the Book to contrast the receptive and the closed, and the verse's three clauses move from the rocks that pour, to the rocks that split, to the rocks that submit, so that the reader ends on the most surprising member of the list. The early teachers read the passage as a description of hearts that had stopped responding after receiving proof, and they placed it beside the signs given to this people in the wilderness. A reader who has heard the same stories and felt nothing new for years should recognise the position he is in.

**THREE KINDS OF STONE, THREE KINDS OF RESPONSE**

The verse sorts stones by their behaviour, and the sorting is a small lesson in itself. One pours out rivers, another breaks open and lets water through, and a third stands in awe of its Maker; the first two are useful, and the third is simply obedient. Human beings who have received a revelation are expected to do at least as much as the rocks they have seen, and the verse's accusation is that they have managed less. The Book uses the same rank in another place where the mountains are described as humbled and the earth as speaking, and it does not treat those images as decoration. What the reader should carry away is not that the comparison is harsh but that it is available: a person who has hardened still has the material of a softer thing inside him, and the verse does not say the condition is permanent.

**THE WARNING IN THE LAST CLAUSE**

The final sentence is short and takes the discussion out of the hands of the people discussing it: God is never unaware of what they do. The Book places this clause after the description of hearts because the audience might otherwise assume that hardness is invisible and costless, a private condition with no consequences attached. The whole section of this sūrah is written against that assumption, since the previous verses have just shown a killer exposed and a concealment revealed. A reader who finds his own heart described in the comparison should read the clause as a comfort as much as a threat, because the One who is aware of the hardness is also the One who can remove it. The verse ends without offering a remedy, and the next verses explain where the hardness came from.

**WHEN THE LIVING CENTRE CEASES TO YIELD**

Think of a person who has been in the same argument for ten years and can no longer hear the other side's sentences as arguments at all; the words arrive as noise and leave without effect. That is the condition the verse describes, and it is not produced by a single event; it is the result of repeated refusal to be moved. The people of this chapter had received water from stone, food from the sky, and a dead man raised in front of them, and the Book's verdict on them is that their hearts came out of it harder than the objects that had obeyed. A reader can test the same condition in himself by noticing what he has stopped responding to: a verse he no longer hears, a warning he has explained away, a duty he has agreed with for years. The Book's answer to a hardening heart is not a new miracle; it is the same message, heard again with the intention of being changed by it. In the present day, repeated exposure to suffering can harden a conscience unless attention is deliberately restored.

---

## Verse 2:75

> Do you ˹believers still˺ expect them to be true to you, though a group of them would hear the word of Allah then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it

**AN EXPECTATION THAT HAS TO BE GIVEN UP**

The verse asks the believers a question about their hopes, and the answer is left with the reader: ***“Do you ˹believers still˺ expect them to be true to you”***, ***“though a group of them would hear the word of Allah”***, ***“then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it”***. The charge is specific, and it is not that this group rejected what it heard; the charge is that the meaning was grasped and then altered deliberately. The believers are being asked why they keep offering trust to people whose practice has already been described, and the question is a correction aimed at the trusting rather than at the untrustworthy. The Book treats misplaced confidence as a fault of its own, since a community that never learns from a pattern of deception will keep paying for the same lesson. The sentence assumes that the record is sufficient evidence and that no further proof is required before a reader adjusts his expectations. Ibn ʿAbbās identified the listeners as a party who heard Moses recite God's words, understood what they heard, and then altered it knowingly, which makes comprehension part of the charge.

**WHAT IT MEANS TO CORRUPT A WORD KNOWINGLY**

The phrase about understanding before altering is the hinge of the verse, because it removes the excuse of ignorance from the offence. A person who changes a text he does not understand may be careless; a person who changes what he has grasped is doing something else, and the Book's later description of that conduct is blunt: (2:79 — **“So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say,”**). The same charge is laid out again elsewhere, in wording that describes the distortion being done with the tongue so that listeners take it for the Book: (3:78 — **“There are some among them”**). The verse therefore does not describe a dispute about interpretation, since interpretation leaves the words in place. It describes a change made to the wording itself by people who knew what the wording had been.

**HOW THIS PEOPLE'S HABIT AFFECTS A READER**

A reader should notice how much of the chapter's account of this community is built on this one charge, since the distortion is named here and returns at the end of the sūrah in a prayer about not being made to bear what others have twisted. The practical consequence for a reader is a caution about trust: an honest disagreement can be worked with, but a group that has been shown to rewrite what it receives cannot be relied upon to convey what it is told. The Book's instruction here is not to hate the people concerned; it is to stop expecting from them a fidelity they have already demonstrated they do not practise. A community that keeps hoping otherwise will find its own message changing in their hands, which is the loss the verse is trying to prevent.

**THE TRUSTING PARTY AND ITS HABIT**

Think of a lender who has been repaid late three times and still counts the fourth promise as reliable, and whose friends have stopped warning him because he does not want to hear it. The Book's question in this verse is the friend's question, and it is asked of the believers because they are the ones who keep extending credit. The verse does not ask them to become suspicious of everyone, since it speaks of a group among the people and not of the whole people; it asks them to calibrate their expectations to what they have seen. The record of the previous verses is the evidence, and anyone who has read the argument so far knows that the question has only one sensible answer. What the Book wants from its own community is a clear-eyed trust, and a clear-eyed trust is one that has been adjusted by experience rather than by wishful thinking.

**A TRUST THAT NEVER LEARNS FROM ITSELF**

There is a wider lesson in the question for any community that carries a message, and it concerns the difference between goodwill and judgement. Goodwill keeps the door open and hopes the best of people, and it is a virtue; judgement notices when the same words are received and returned differently, and it is a duty that goodwill needs. The people described in this verse had the scripture in their hands and the understanding of it in their heads, and they chose to pass on something else, which is why the verse names the knowing as the aggravating factor. A reader who keeps a record of his own dealings can see the value of the Book's sharpness here, since the community that learns from one deception will not need to learn from the same deception again. The verse closes the question without answering it, and the silence is the answer. Today, selective quotation can alter a message without changing every word, especially when an audience never checks the full record.

---

## Verse 2:76

> When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.” But in private they say ˹to each other˺, “Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you, so that they may use it against you before your Lord? Do you not understand?”

**TWO CONVERSATIONS IN THE SAME DAY**

The verse draws a room with two doors, and the same people are heard through each of them: ***“When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.””***, ***“But in private they say ˹to each other˺, “Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you”***, ***“so that they may use it against you before your Lord?”***, ***“Do you not understand?””*** The public sentence is short and warm, and the private one is a warning to keep quiet, which means the people speaking know exactly what they are doing. What they fear is not violence or exposure in the ordinary sense; it is that the knowledge they hold will be turned into evidence in an argument they cannot win. The chapter has already shown the same people in the same double posture earlier, where their public claim is reported word for word and their private one is a confession of mockery: (2:14 — **“But when alone with their evil associates they say, “We are definitely with you;”**). The verse in front of the reader supplies the motive that the earlier one only hinted at. Ibn ʿAbbās read the scene as a split between public recognition among the believers and private rebuke from leaders who feared that disclosed knowledge would become evidence against them.

**DISCLOSED FACTS TREATED AS LIABILITY**

The thing they are guarding is described as knowledge that has been revealed to them, and that description is the verse's sharpest point. They are not hiding a sin or a private opinion; they are hiding scriptural material, and their reason is that it bears witness to the truth the believers are preaching. A later sūrah records a similar concealment in plainer words, where a party of the People of the Book is described as distorting what they carry and passing it off as revelation: (3:78 — **“who distort the Book with their tongues to make you think this ˹distortion˺ is”**). The counsel given in private is therefore not a strategy for survival; it is a decision to suppress evidence, and the verse allows the reader to hear it being made. Their question at the end, asking whether the others understand, is ironic, since understanding is exactly what they have and are deciding to bury.

**THE BILL FOR SPEAKING IN TWO VOICES**

The passage is a study in the price of speaking in two voices, and the price is paid in the speaker's own character before it is paid anywhere else. A person who says one thing in a room and another in a corridor has to keep track of two audiences, two vocabularies, and two accounts of his own position, and the effort is spent on management rather than belief. The Book treats this condition as a sickness rather than as cleverness, and it gives its own verdict on those who practise it in the chapter's earlier portrait of the hypocrites. The community that hears both sentences is confused for a while, but the confusion does not last, because the private sentence eventually becomes the practice. The verse shows the mechanism in operation, and the reader can see where the second voice will lead before the chapter says so directly.

**COUNSEL OFFERED BEHIND A DOOR**

Think of a person in a workplace who agrees with the proposal in the meeting and then texts a colleague that the whole thing is nonsense, and who believes that the two remarks are separate events. The Book's report from this verse is that the private remark is the real position, and the public one is the price of admission. The people described here had a further motive, because the knowledge in their hands could have settled the argument, and their fear of being used against made them suppress it. A reader can identify the same trade in himself whenever he knows something that would change a discussion and keeps it back for the sake of his standing. The Book's closing question about understanding addresses that reader as much as the group in the room.

**THE UNDERSTANDING THEY DENIED TO OTHERS**

The verse ends with a question, which is the Book's way of letting the people condemn themselves out of their own mouths. They ask whether their colleagues understand that disclosure would be dangerous, and the answer the Book implies is that they have understood the wrong thing entirely: what is dangerous is not the truth but the concealment. The same pattern appears wherever a group decides that its position matters more than its evidence, and the outcome is always a community that has to keep its own members in the dark. The reader who wants a test can take the sentence he would most dislike being repeated in public and ask why, since the answer is usually the thing this verse is about. The Book does not need to accuse anyone further; it has simply recorded the two conversations and left the reader to decide which one he would rather have spoken. Present-day organisations repeat the scene when junior members admit a fact publicly and senior figures scold them for weakening the approved story.

---

## Verse 2:77

> Do they not know that Allah is aware of what they conceal and what they reveal

**A ROOM THAT WAS NEVER PRIVATE**

The question that closes the previous verse is answered by a second question, and the answer removes the room the people thought they were standing in: ***“Do they not know”***, ***“that Allah is aware of what they conceal”***, ***“and what they reveal”***. The two halves cover everything a person can do with information, since concealment and disclosure between them describe the whole range of human speech, and the verse says that both are known. The counsel given in private was a decision about what to say in front of which audience, and the verse tells the reader that the audience had been larger than they thought. Nothing in the sentence is new information about the people in the room; the Book is reminding them of what a monotheist is supposed to have understood already. That is why the question begins with knowledge rather than accusation: the failure described is not a failure of information but of attention. Ibn ʿAbbās applied the two clauses to leaders whose concealed counsel and public speech differed, while both remained equally open to divine knowledge.

**WHY CONCEALMENT FEELS SAFE**

A person hides a thing because he believes that a closed door changes the situation, and the belief is practical and almost universal. The verse does not deny the usefulness of discretion; it denies that discretion creates a space where conduct is unobserved, and the point is made throughout the Book in the same terms. Another passage reports the same mistake in a case where the concealment was more elaborate and the plotters more confident: (4:108 — **“They try to hide ˹their deception˺ from people,”**). The people in this sūrah were afraid that their knowledge would be used as evidence before God, which is a remarkable fear for a group who also believed that God knows everything. Their conduct shows the difference between a belief held in the mind and a belief that shapes what a person does in a corridor.

**THE TWO HALVES OF A SINGLE RECORD**

The pairing of the concealed and the revealed is a feature of the Book's language about knowledge, and it appears wherever a community needs reminding that its inner and outer life are one record. The readers of this page are told elsewhere that God knows the deceit of the eyes and what the hearts conceal, and the same theme runs through the section of this sūrah that deals with the hypocrites. What makes this verse useful is its economy: a single sentence covers the whispers in the room and the declaration in the street without distinguishing between them, so no reader is left with a corner he can keep. The practical effect of believing this is not anxiety but honesty, since a person who has stopped managing his secrecy has less to manage overall. The verse treats that freedom as the natural state of someone who knows who is present.

**AN OPEN LINE IN A CLOSED OFFICE**

Think of the day a person discovers that a microphone in the meeting room has been live for months, and of how quickly his recollection of that period rearranges itself around the sentences he would not have said. The Book's reminder in this verse is that the situation is permanent, and that the knowledge belongs to the One who is addressed in every prayer a person makes. A reader can test his own understanding of that by noticing what he says when he is certain that only friends are listening, since that is the register in which he actually speaks. The verse does not ask a person to behave as though he were being watched; it tells him that he is, which is a different and simpler instruction. When the fact is accepted, the two conversations of the previous verse collapse into one.

**PRIVATE AND PUBLIC UNDER ONE JUDGEMENT**

The instruction hidden inside the question is that a reader should let his private speech be judged by the same standard as his public speech, since no audience is really narrower. The people of the verse had two reasons to keep up their double talk, and the Book's answer addresses both by removing the only conditions that made it seem worth doing. A community whose members hold this belief will be difficult to deceive from inside, because there is nothing to gain from a secret that is not secret. This sentence closes the discussion of concealed speech and prepares the next passage about people who speculate about the Book without knowledge, and it does its work with a single sentence and a question. A reader who has taken it seriously will find that it simplifies his conduct rather than complicating it. Today, private messages and public statements may have different audiences, but neither has a different moral owner.

---

## Verse 2:78

> And among them are the illiterate who know nothing about the Scripture except lies, and ˹so˺ they ˹wishfully˺ speculate

**THE UNLETTERED AND THEIR WISHFUL STORIES**

The chapter turns from the people who altered the text to the people who never had it: ***“And among them are the illiterate”***, ***“who know nothing about the Scripture except lies”***, ***“and ˹so˺ they ˹wishfully˺ speculate”***. The word translated here as the illiterate describes people who could not read a book at all, and what they possess instead of a text is a set of claims they hope are true. The Book distinguishes them from the group described in the previous verse, because the learned who changed the words and the unlettered who repeat the changes are not the same offenders. What the reader is shown is a two-storey arrangement: a written tradition being edited above and a spoken one being invented below, with the second depending on the first for its authority. The verse's last word is about guessing, and the whole tragedy of the passage is that people with no access to the Book are confident about what it says. The same kind of untested hope is named later in this sūrah, where two communities at once claim the future for themselves: (2:111 — **“The Jews and Christians each claim”**). Ibn ʿAbbās understood the unlettered as people unable to read the Scripture for themselves and the wishes as unsupported tales received from leaders and repeated as guesses.

**THE TALES THAT WERE EASY TO BELIEVE**

The claims held by the unlettered are described as wishes, which tells the reader how they survived: they were pleasant, they flattered the community, and nobody in a position to check them had an interest in doing so. A later sūrah reports the same community in the same posture, generations after the covenant, still working from inherited claims that had never been tested against the text: (7:169 — **“Then they were succeeded by other generations”**). The Book's charge against the educated is that they knowingly corrupted the words; its charge against the ordinary people is that they were content with comfortable guesses. Neither charge is about a lack of intelligence, and neither is excused by the other. A community in which knowledge is handled by a small group and never verified by the rest will produce exactly this division, and the Book records the result without surprise.

**INHERITED TALES LEFT UNCHECKED**

Think of a family that has repeated for three generations that a particular piece of property was a gift and never a loan, and that discovers after a death that the document says otherwise. The people repeating the claim are honest, and the claim is still wrong, and the person who benefits from the error is not necessarily the one who invented it. The illiterate of this verse were the last link in that chain, and the Book places them in a chapter about covenant-breaking because a community's belief is carried by its unexamined commonplaces as much as by its scholars. A reader who wants to apply the verse does not need to find an illiterate man; he needs to find the beliefs he holds about his own religion that he has never once checked against a text, because the wishful claim survives precisely as long as nobody opens the book.

**THE DUTY OF THE UNLEARNED AND THE GUILT OF THE LEARNED**

The passage distributes responsibility with a precision that is worth copying in any community. The people who cannot read are not blamed for failing to read; they are blamed for speculating, which is something they could have declined to do. The people who can read are blamed for altering what they had, which is a different offence with a heavier penalty named in the next verse. This distribution protects the weak and indicts the strong, and it leaves no one with the excuse that his education was limited. The same Book tells its own community that the believers must ask and learn rather than speculate, and it places the burden of teaching on those who hold the knowledge. Where a community has stopped teaching, the Book's account of this people shows what grows in the space.

**A SPECULATION THAT BECAME A CREED**

The verse is short, and it describes a process that takes decades. A claim invented to explain an awkward text, repeated by people who trust the teller, becomes the settled belief of a village, and then the belief is defended as tradition by people who have never seen the text. By the time anyone checks, the correction sounds like an attack on the community, which is why the Book records the sequence at the point where the blame is still traceable. The reader's defence against the process is the same in every era, and it is unglamorous: check the claim against the source before it becomes part of a person. The unlettered in this verse were not condemned for what they could not do, and the reader who has the means to check is in a stronger position than they were, which raises the standard rather than lowering it. In the present day, forwarded claims can become communal certainty when those unable to verify them are taught that repetition is knowledge. Therefore the blame is distributed with care: leaders answer for invention, while hearers answer for turning untested wishes into certainty.

---

## Verse 2:79

> So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say, “This is from Allah”—seeking a fleeting gain! So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they have earned

**A CURSE ON THOSE WHO WRITE AND LIE**

The next verse names the offence and pronounces on it twice: ***“So woe to those”***, ***“who distort the Scripture with their own hands”***, ***“then say, “This is from Allah””***, ***“seeking a fleeting gain!”***, ***“So woe to them”***, ***“for what their hands have written”***, ***“and woe to them”***, ***“for what they have earned”***. The charge is not that a text was copied badly; it is that hands wrote something and a mouth attributed it to God for a price. The Book's double woe separates the two halves of the crime, so that the writing and the gain are each answered on their own. What makes the verse heavy is the audience: the people doing this were not outsiders attacking a scripture; they were the ones entrusted with it, and the thing they sold was the authority of the One who had given it. The Book keeps a place for the same instinct in another charge about people who raise themselves above the truth they were given: (4:49 — **“Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who ˹falsely˺ elevate themselves?”**). Ibn ʿAbbās read the small gain as livelihood and property acquired through alteration, making the repeated woe answer both the forged writing and the unlawful earnings it produced.

**THE FEE THAT MADE THE FRAUD WORTH IT**

The verse describes the motive in two words, and it is not large: a small, passing profit. A person who rewrites a verse for a fee is not buying an empire; the Book's choice of words tells the reader how cheaply the traders valued what they had. The same subject comes up elsewhere in the sūrah where concealment of the Book is traded for a little gain, and the pattern the Book lays out is that the sellers are always convinced the sum is modest and reasonable. A reader can test the arithmetic in his own work, since the compromises that damage a community are almost never made for a fortune. They are made for a favour, a position, or the avoidance of an awkward conversation, and the Book lists the consequence beside the price so the reader can see the imbalance.

**THE HANDS AND THE MOUTH**

The verse locates the crime in two parts of the body, and the pairing is deliberate. The hands write what was not given, and the mouth supplies the attribution, which means the forgery requires the cooperation of both the maker and the speaker. This is why the Book does not describe the offence as a slip of the pen; a written change becomes a lie only when it is presented as revelation, and both steps were taken knowingly. The same image appears in a passage that warns those who read a fabricated text to an audience that cannot check it, and it appears again among the charges laid against this people in the chapters that follow. A reader who handles religious material in any form is being shown the two moments at which the offence is committed, and both moments are available to him.

**THE GAINS THAT ARE GONE BY MORNING**

Think of a clerk who copies a land record with one measurement altered, and whose fee for the alteration is modest, and who then lives with the result for the rest of his life. The verse's phrase about a fleeting gain is a reminder of the time horizon, since the Book regularly measures profit against what remains after it is spent. The people in this passage were paid in standing, influence, or income, and none of those currencies is recognised on the day the Book keeps describing. The double woe at the end covers both the document and the career built on it, so that no part of the transaction escapes the sentence. A reader who wants the verse to be about him rather than about a distant scribe can begin with the question of what he would alter in his testimony if the price were right.

**THE WRITING AND THE PROFIT JUDGED TOGETHER**

The structure of the verse gives the reader a rule about deception in religious matters: the falsification and the benefit always arrive together, and the Book names them together so that neither can be hidden behind the other. A community that tolerates edited scripture for the sake of a smooth relationship has bought the same arrangement at one remove, since the income from a lie is not always money. The passage ends here, and the next verse begins a new accusation about the claims this community makes about its own future, which shows how one corruption prepares the ground for the next. What a reader takes away is not only a warning about forgery but a test he can run on the material he receives: where a claim about God arrives with an advantage attached, the Book's verdict on the transaction is already written. Today, fabricated religious claims can still purchase influence, donations or access, making the small gain recognisable in modern forms.

---

## Verse 2:80

> ˹Some of˺ the Jews claim, “The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Have you taken a pledge from Allah—for Allah never breaks His word—or are you ˹just˺ saying about Allah what you do not know?”

**A CLAIM ABOUT THE FIRE AND THREE QUESTIONS**

The verse reports a doctrine the community had settled on for itself, and then answers it with questions: ***“˹Some of˺ the Jews claim, “The Fire will not touch us except”***, ***“for a number of days.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Have you taken a pledge from Allah”***, ***“for Allah never breaks His word”***, ***“or are you ˹just˺ saying about Allah what you do not know?””*** The claim is that the punishment will be brief, and the reply does not dispute the length; it asks where the length came from. A person may hold a doctrine about the Day of Judgement only if he has been given a promise about it, and the verse's first question establishes that a promise from God would have been honoured. The second question then separates the two possibilities left: either the community holds a contract it cannot produce, or it is speaking about God without knowledge, and the reader is free to choose which description fits. Ibn ʿAbbās transmitted the claim as forty days in the Fire, matched to the days of calf worship, and read the reply as a demand for a covenant that their own Scripture did not contain.

**THE DOCTRINE AS IT IS MET ELSEWHERE**

The Book reports this confident arithmetic about the Fire in more than one place, which tells the reader that it was a settled feature of the community's self-understanding rather than a slip of the tongue. In a later sūrah the claim is repeated with the number left vague and the consequence spelled out, since the Book treats the wish as the source of the deception: (3:24 — **“This is because they say, “The Fire will not touch us except”**). Another passage shows the claim being tested by an invitation, which is the Book's usual method with people who are certain about their own standing: (62:6 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O Jews!”**). The repetition matters for a reader because it shows the claim doing work in the community: it was not a private hope but a public doctrine, and it shaped how people behaved toward their own misconduct.

**A HOPE DRESSED AS A GUARANTEE**

The reply in this verse is a piece of reasoning that a reader can reuse, and it turns on the difference between a hope and a guarantee. If God had promised a short punishment for this community, the promise would be kept, since the Book says plainly that His word is never broken. What the verse then exposes is a claim made without such a promise, and the Book's word for that is speech about God without knowledge, which it treats as a serious matter in its own right. The doctrine was comforting, and comfort is not evidence; the question in the verse is designed to make the claimants notice the difference before they are asked to rely on it. A reader who holds any opinion about his own standing on the Day can run the same two questions over it, and he will find that most such opinions are hopes wearing the clothes of knowledge.

**A DOCTRINE THAT MAKES PEOPLE COMFORTABLE**

Think of a firm whose managers have convinced themselves that the inspection will pass because they have always passed, and whose confidence grows with each year in which nothing was examined. The same kind of assurance had been built here on a claim that nobody could trace to a source, and the Book's answer removes the assurance without removing the hope: a person may hope for mercy, and he may not announce terms for it. The difference between the two is the difference between humility and presumption, and the Book treats the second as a form of lying about God. A reader who has heard this claim discussed as though it were a settled arrangement can see how the verse dismantles it, and he can also see how easily the same structure rebuilds itself inside any religious community.

**THE UNSUPPORTED GUARANTEE EXPOSED**

The verse ends with the phrase about speaking without knowledge, and the phrase is the reason this passage sits where it does in the sūrah. The previous verses described people who altered the scripture and people who speculated about it, and this verse shows the fruit of both: a doctrine about the Last Day held with confidence and no evidence. The Book's remedy is not silence but knowledge, since it asks the community to test its claims against what has actually been given. A reader who takes the instruction seriously will find that the question is portable, and that it applies to the doctrines he inherited from his family as much as to the ones he chose himself. What the verse refuses to allow is the sentence that sounds like certainty without a source behind it. Present-day spiritual confidence is equally unsafe when it rests on an imagined exception rather than a promise God actually made.

---

## Verse 2:81

> But no! Those who commit evil and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever

**A CORRECTION: EVIL IS NOT A SHORT VISIT**

Two words end the discussion that the previous verse's confidence had opened: ***“But no! Those who commit evil”***, ***“and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever”***. The Book's denial is total, and its correction is not about arithmetic; it replaces a term of days with a permanence, and it attaches that permanence to a condition rather than to a lineage. The people described are those who have been enveloped by their misdeeds, and the image is of something that has closed over the offender rather than of a single act recorded against him. That distinction is the verse's real subject, since it separates the person who slips and returns from the person whose conduct has become the atmosphere he lives in. The claim about a limited punishment is answered by a description of a life that was never limited. Ibn ʿAbbās read the surrounding sin as evil carried without repentance until death, which is why the verse describes residence rather than a passing punishment.

**SIN CLOSING AROUND ITS MAKER**

The phrase translated here as engrossed or enveloped carries the sense of a thing that surrounds a person on every side, and the early teachers read it as a description of a man whose bad deeds have become his environment. This is a different category from the person who errs, regrets, and corrects himself, and the Book keeps the two apart in almost every passage about punishment. The same permanence is stated in another place where the residents of the Fire are named and their stay described without a term: (2:39 — **“But those who disbelieve”**). A reader who wants the verse to apply to someone else should notice that the condition is measured by what a person's life has become, which is not a judgement he can make about another man's interior. The Book's warning lands on the one person whose conduct he can actually inspect.

**WHY PERMANENCE IS THE RIGHT ANSWER TO PRESUMPTION**

The community had claimed a term of days, and the Book answers with forever, and the answer is not arbitrary. A person who has decided in advance how long his punishment will last has decided that his conduct cannot reach a certain severity, and that decision is itself a form of presumption about God. The claim was comfortable and it made repentance less urgent, which is exactly what the Book is warning against in this passage. The next verse sets the believers beside this description, and the contrast shows that the permanence is attached to a state of being and not to a label. A reader who takes the correction seriously will stop negotiating the terms of a judgement that has not yet happened and start examining the conduct that would determine them.

**A FLOODED ROOM AND THE WATER NOBODY NOTICES**

Think of a household that has stopped noticing the water rising through its own floor, and whose members argue about whether the damp will last the winter. The verse's word for being engrossed describes the people in that house, and the Book's answer to their argument is that the water is not seasonal. The comparison is uncomfortable because it suggests that the community's debate about the duration of punishment was itself a symptom, since a person whose conduct had not swallowed him would not be calculating the length of the penalty. A reader who finds that he has an opinion ready about how long he would deserve to be punished has already begun the calculation, and the verse invites him to set it down and look at the state of the room instead. The Book's treatment of the claim is therefore an examination of the claimant.

**THE RESIDENTS NAMED AND THE ALTERNATIVE HELD BACK**

The verse ends with a description and leaves the reader to turn the page for its counterpart, which is a structure the Book uses often and which keeps the reader moving. What has been established here is that the permanence of the Fire is tied to a life that has been taken over by wrongdoing, and that a claim to a shorter term is a claim about one's own case. The passage does not tell a reader how to measure the degree of envelopment in his own life, and no measure is required of him, because the Book's guidance throughout the sūrah has been to act on what is clear and to leave the accounting to God. The following verse names those who live in the Garden forever, and the two verses together form a single picture with the reader standing between them. What he does next is the subject of the rest of the chapter. Today, repeated wrongdoing can surround a life gradually, one defended choice at a time, before the person notices what has become normal.

---

## Verse 2:82

> And those who believe and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever

**THE ANSWER SET BESIDE THE WARNING**

The previous verse described a condition and its end, and this one takes the same shape and turns it toward the opposite kind of life: ***“And those who believe”***, ***“and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever”***. Faith and good conduct are named in the order the Book keeps using, since the deed grows out of the belief rather than replacing it. What is permanent on this side of the sentence is a residence rather than a visit, and the pairing of the two verses is the chapter's way of showing that the same scale measures both outcomes. The reader who has just been told what happens to a life swallowed by wrongdoing is now told what happens to a life spent doing the good that faith produced, and both statements are addressed to people who can still choose. The Book makes the same invitation to hurry toward that residence in another sūrah: (3:133 — **“And hasten towards forgiveness from your Lord and a Paradise as vast”**). Ibn ʿAbbās joined belief to acts of obedience and understood the lasting residence as life without death or expulsion, the exact opposite of the condition just described.

**TWO DESTINATIONS WRITTEN SIDE BY SIDE**

A reader might wonder why the Book does not separate the two destinations, and the answer lies in the way it teaches. Placing them side by side prevents the reader from holding one without the other, so that the warning and the promise arrive in the same reading and the imagination has to work on both. The pair also protects the reader from the mistake of the previous passage, since a community that had decided on a short punishment for itself could have used a verse about mercy as a licence. The Book's habit is to state the door and the pit together, and later it places a similar description of the Garden's residents in similar terms and the description comes directly after the fate of their opposites: (98:7 — **“Indeed, those who believe and do good—they”**). A reader who only collects the promises has misunderstood the pattern the Book is using.

**WHAT RESIDENCE MEANS AS A PICTURE**

The word for residency in this pair of verses is not the same as the word for a long stay; it carries the sense of belonging to a place and remaining in it. Ownership of a home changes a person's relation to it, and the Book uses the image because it is the clearest way to describe a permanence that is also a privilege. In the present world the same term is used for the settlement of a community in a land, and the reader is being told that the life to come is not a campsite. The picture is completed later in the sūrah with descriptions of gardens, rivers, and companions, and those images come from the same desire to give an idea a shape the reader can hold. What matters here is that the promise is stated in terms of a settled condition rather than a moment of reward.

**TWO FAMILIES IN THE SAME CORRIDOR**

Think of two families waiting on the same morning for the outcome of a case that will decide where they live, and of how differently the same corridor feels to each of them. The Book's pairing of these two verses creates that corridor for the reader, and it does so without describing the argument or the judge, because the two sentences are enough. The reader's task is not to decide who occupies which room but to notice that the question of his own life is being asked in the same hearing. A person who can hold both sentences in his mind at once has acquired something valuable, since most self-deception works by keeping one of them out of view. The Book closes the door on that trick by writing them one after the other.

**CONDUCT THAT CONFIRMS BELIEF**

The second clause of the verse is a description of a life and not of a single act, and the Book's word for it covers everything a person does in accordance with what he believes. The verse's general wording is deliberate, since no list of prayers, charities, or fasts is given here, although the sūrah names them in other places; the general word is used to keep the promise open to every good deed a reader performs. The pairing with belief also rules out the notion that good conduct can stand on its own as a substitute for faith, since the deed is named as the fruit of a root. A reader who wants to test his own position can ask what his conduct has grown out of, because the Book's interest is in the tree rather than in the fruit alone. The verse ends where the chapter's other promises end, with a permanence given to those who believe and act on their belief. In the present day, belief becomes visible through honest work, kept trusts and quiet service rather than through identity alone.

---

## Verse 2:83

> And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel ˹stating˺, “Worship none but Allah; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy; speak kindly to people; establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.” But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away—except for a few of you—and were indifferent

**TERMS THAT NAMED THE WEAK FIRST**

The pledge taken from this people is read out here in its own words: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel ˹stating˺, “Worship none”***, ***“but Allah; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans”***, ***“and the needy”***, ***“speak kindly to people”***, ***“establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.””***, ***“But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away”***, ***“except for a few of you”***, ***“and were indifferent”***. The list is remarkable for what it puts beside the worship of God, since it names parents, kin, orphans, the poor, and then every person a speaker might address. A covenant in the ancient world usually bound a people to a king and settled what they owed him; this one binds them to a set of obligations whose beneficiaries are mostly people without power. The worship of the One comes first and the treatment of the weak comes second, and the Book does not separate the two into different documents. The same covenant is recalled in another sūrah with the leaders appointed to witness it: (5:12 — **“Allah made a covenant with the Children of Israel”**). Ibn ʿAbbās unfolded the covenant as exclusive worship, dutiful care for parents and kin, generosity to the vulnerable, truthful speech, prayer and the due share of wealth.

**THE ORDER OF THE TERMS AND WHY IT MATTERS**

The sequence begins with the exclusivity of worship and moves outward in circles of decreasing closeness, and the arrangement is not accidental. A person who has settled the question of whom he serves is then asked about those who depend on him, starting with his parents and widening to strangers; the Book elsewhere repeats almost the same list in almost the same order when it wants to describe the good life: (4:36 — **“Worship Allah ˹alone˺ and associate none with Him.”**). The movement from the divine to the domestic is a warning against a piety that stops at the first item, since the Book treats a claim of devotion that leaves the household and the street untouched as incomplete. The same chapter teaches that righteousness is not a matter of turning toward one direction or another but of what a person does with what he has: (2:177 — **“Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east”**). The terms of the covenant are therefore a single fabric, and the reader who pulls on one thread will find the others attached.

**KINDNESS TO PARENTS AS A COMMANDMENT IN THE MIDDLE OF A LIST**

Among the items stands a command that the Book repeats in its own right in another sūrah, where honouring parents is joined to the decree that God alone is to be worshipped: (17:23 — **“For your Lord has decreed that you worship none”**). The inclusion of orphans and the needy in the same sentence is a reminder that a community's treatment of those without protectors is one of the measures the Book applies to it repeatedly. The verse then reports that the children of Israel walked away from these terms and were indifferent, and the word for indifference covers the whole attitude: not hostility, not denial, but the condition of someone who has heard the terms and cannot be moved. The Book's charge is therefore not only that a people broke a rule but that they stopped caring about the obligations placed on them.

**A CHECKLIST A READER CAN USE**

Think of a man who keeps the fasts, attends the congregation, and has not spoken to his own mother in two years, and who would describe himself without hesitation as a religious person. The covenant in this verse is arranged to catch exactly that inconsistency, because it places the worship of God and the duty to parents in one sentence and makes the reader deal with both at once. The Book does not claim that the second earns the first or that the first excuses the second; it lists them as parts of one agreement, and it reports the consequences of treating the agreement as a menu. A reader who wants an honest reading can take the six items in the verse as a checklist for the coming week and see how much of his religion survives the exercise. The Book's charge against the people in this passage was indifference, and the remedy for indifference is a concrete act performed where it is visible.

**THE FEW WHO DID NOT TURN AWAY**

The verse does not end in an accusation without exception; it records that a few of the people kept to the covenant, and the Book's habit of noting the remnant is one of its most consistent mercies. The majority turned away and were indifferent, and the few who did not are named in a single clause that has kept hope for the community in every generation since. The same pattern appears where the Book says that some among them were upright and recited the revelations at night, and where the reader is warned against treating a whole people as a single character. What the reader should take from the clause is that the covenant remained available and that fidelity was possible inside the same community that broke it. The chapter's argument never becomes a condemnation of a lineage; it stays a matter of what each person does with the terms he has been given.

**WORSHIP AND THE STREET IN ONE SENTENCE**

The lasting value of this passage for a reader of any community is its refusal to separate devotion from conduct. The list in the verse begins in the sanctuary and ends in the marketplace, and the same movement occurs in the chapter's later teaching about spending, giving, and dealing fairly. The people addressed had a covenant whose terms they knew, and they turned away from a document that asked them to be kind to orphans and to speak well to others, which is a remarkable thing to abandon. A reader who finds himself drawn to the first term and reluctant about the rest can see in this verse what the Book thinks of a religion with one item left. The few who kept the whole list are mentioned, and the reader is invited to count himself among them. Today, devotion is tested at the bedside of a parent, in speech to a stranger and in the handling of money owed to the poor.

---

## Verse 2:84

> And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant that you would neither shed each other’s blood nor expel each other from their homes, you gave your pledge and bore witness

**A SECOND PLEDGE ABOUT BLOOD AND HOMES**

The covenant in this verse is more specific than the list before it, and it deals with the two things a community does to itself: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant”***, ***“that you would neither shed each other's blood”***, ***“nor expel each other from their homes, you gave your pledge”***, ***“and bore witness”***. The terms forbid killing inside the community and the driving out of neighbours from their houses, and the verse then records that the people accepted the terms and testified to them. That final clause is the reason the next verse is so severe, because a pledge that has been openly witnessed cannot be broken by mistake. The Book has moved from the duties owed to the weak to the duties owed to one another, and it is building a record in which the community's own agreement is the evidence against it. The pledge taken from this people is recalled again where the messengers sent to them are named beside it: (5:70 — **“Indeed, We took a covenant from the Children of Israel and sent them messengers.”**). Ibn ʿAbbās applied the prohibition of bloodshed and expulsion to members of the same people, and linked the historical breach to the rival Madinan groups later named in the dispute.

**LIFE AND HOME UNDER THE SAME PLEDGE**

The verse protects life and it protects the home, which are the two things a person cannot replace by his own effort, and the Book names them together because they are usually threatened together. A community at war with itself does not simply kill; it drives families out, and the exile that follows is often slower than the violence it avoids. The terms of this covenant are therefore a set of walls around the whole group, and the Book treats the agreement as a settled matter that the people had already accepted. The same charges are laid out in another passage among the reasons a people was condemned, where covenant-breaking stands at the head of the list: (4:155 — **“˹They were condemned˺ for breaking their covenant, rejecting Allah's signs,”**). A reader can see the Book building its case with the community's own words, since the pledge and the testimony are recorded in the same sentence as the offence that follows.

**THE WEIGHT OF A WITNESSED PLEDGE**

The closing words of this verse are easy to read past, and they carry the whole argument of the passage. Bearing witness is a voluntary act, and a person who has testified to an agreement has placed his own credibility inside it, so that the breaking of the terms becomes a matter of his honesty as well as his conduct. The Book's law later requires witnesses for contracts precisely because a witnessed agreement can be enforced, and this verse supplies the most solemn possible witness. The people had given their word twice over, once in speech and once in testimony, which is why the next verse can ask them how they came to be doing the very things they had promised to avoid. The reader who follows the Book's argument here will notice that the exposure depends on the community's own record rather than on an outside accusation.

**A STREET THAT SIGNED AND THEN BUILT GATES**

Think of a street whose residents have signed an agreement that nobody will build a wall across the common path, and who then, one by one, put up gates and shut the newer families out of the square. The Book's account of this people uses the same structure: a written pledge, a public witness, and then a slow reversal in practice that everyone can see and nobody will name. The offence in the verse is not an isolated act of violence but a condition that had come to be accepted, since the next verse describes people who kill and expel while continuing to ransom their captives. The Book's charge is that the community kept the ceremonies of the covenant while dismantling its substance, and the reader who has watched a group treat a promise as a formality knows the pattern. A person can test himself by listing the agreements he has signed and asking which of them he no longer treats as binding.

**WITNESSED TERMS BECOME THE MEASURE**

The verse establishes that this community will be judged by its own covenant and not by an external standard, and the Book keeps to that principle throughout the passage. The terms were known, the pledge was given, and the testimony was recorded, so the argument that follows needs no further evidence and the reader meets it as a matter of the community's own word. A reader who belongs to a community that carries a scripture is in the same position, since the terms he has accepted are also available in writing and his own profession of them is a form of testimony. The Book's use of this material is not a history lesson aimed at another people; it is a demonstration of how a record of obligations is kept and used. The next verse opens the account of how this particular record was treated, and the question it raises can be heard by any reader who has a pledge of his own. Present-day communities violate the same joined protection when they condemn violence yet support the forced removal of unwanted neighbours.

---

## Verse 2:85

> But here you are, killing each other and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin and aggression; and when those ˹expelled˺ come to you as captives, you still ransom them—though expelling them was unlawful for you. Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest? Is there any reward for those who do so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment? For Allah is never unaware of what you do

**HALF A PLEDGE AND A FULL PRICE**

The accusation arrives with a contrast, and every clause of it is a picture: ***“But here you are, killing each other”***, ***“and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin”***, ***“and aggression; and when those ˹expelled˺ come to you”***, ***“as captives, you still ransom them”***, ***“though expelling them was unlawful”***, ***“for you. Do you believe in some of the Scripture”***, ***“and reject the rest?”***. The same community that had pledged not to spill its own blood is doing it, and the same community that ransomed its captives is the one that put them in chains. The Book's charge is not that they kept nothing of the covenant; it is that they kept the clause that cost little and honoured them, and discarded the clause that protected the people they had decided to fight. The question that ends the sentence is the sharpest in the passage, and it exposes a way of handling a scripture that survives in every generation. The pledge they were breaking is recorded in the verse before this one: (2:84 — **“And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant”**). Ibn ʿAbbās read the contradiction as ransoming captives because Scripture required it while helping to expel those same people despite the equally binding prohibition.

**THE RANSOM THAT EXPOSED THE CONTRADICTION**

Ransoming captives was a recognised duty under the law given to this people, and the verse names it because the practice proves that the community still regarded the scripture as authoritative in the matters it liked. The Book's argument turns on that admission: a people who will pay money to free a captive from their own nation have already accepted the law that made him a brother, and cannot then claim that driving him out was permitted. The same inconsistency is described elsewhere in the sūrah where the community's leaders are shown treating part of what they were given as binding and part as negotiable: (5:44 — **“Indeed, We revealed the Torah, containing guidance and light,”**). What the verse reveals is a habit of selective obedience, and it is the habit rather than any single crime that the Book sets out to correct in this passage on the covenant.

**WHY SELECTIVE FAITH IS TREATED AS UNBELIEF**

The final question uses the language of belief and rejection, and the reader might wonder why a partial acceptance deserves that vocabulary. The answer is in the structure of the verse: the people were not accepting a set of rules and doubting others; they were using the rules they kept as evidence of their standing while breaking the ones that interfered. The Book treats that as a decision about who has authority over a person, and it says as much when it accuses them of rejecting what does not suit them. The same charge is laid in another passage where the object of the trade is named as the covenant itself: (3:77 — **“Indeed, those who trade Allah's covenant”**). A person can test the charge by looking for the command he has quietly granted an exemption and asking what that exemption is worth in the currency the Book uses.

**DISGRACE IN THIS LIFE, PUNISHMENT AFTER**

The verse does not leave the offence without a stated consequence, and it divides the consequence into two instalments.
